sections.subtopic: Classical & Electronic Concepts and Oxidation Numbers
sections.title: Redox as one inseparable transaction: the classical & electronic lenses

board_events.text: REDOX is a single, inseparable transaction
One species gives; another takes — at the very same instant.
Lens 1 — Classical (oxygen / hydrogen) view
Oxidation = adding oxygen or removing hydrogen; reduction is the reverse.
Oxygen is added to magnesium, so magnesium is oxidised. But this lens fails when a reaction has no O or H.
Lens 2 — Electronic view (the deeper truth)
OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

segments.text: Let's open with one picture that ties the whole chapter together. <curious> Picture a busy kirana shop at closing time: the shopkeeper hands over a packet of dal and, in the very same motion, the customer's cash lands in the drawer.

You cannot have a sale without a purchase. Redox reactions work exactly like this — every time one species gives something away, another takes it at the same instant. There is no giving floating around without a taker.
Chemists viewed this transaction through three lenses, each more powerful than the last. Lens one is the oldest — the classical view.
Here, oxidation means adding oxygen or removing hydrogen, and reduction is exactly the reverse.
Watch magnesium burn: two magnesium plus oxygen gives two magnesium oxide.
Oxygen has been added to the magnesium, so magnesium is oxidised. Neat — but this lens collapses the moment a reaction contains no oxygen and no hydrogen at all.
So we sharpen the idea. Lens two says the real event underneath is electron transfer.
Take zinc plus copper two plus giving zinc two plus plus copper. No oxygen, no hydrogen — yet zinc loses two electrons and the copper ion gains them.
And that hands us the most famous mnemonic in the chapter: <excited> O I L R I G — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain, of electrons.

Chapter की शुरुआत एक picture से, जो पूरे topic को जोड़ता है। <curious> एक busy kirana shop सोचो closing time पे: shopkeeper दाल का packet देता है, और उसी motion में customer का cash drawer में आ जाता है।
Sale बिना purchase के हो ही नहीं सकती। Redox reaction बिल्कुल ऐसे ही है — जब भी एक species कुछ देती है, दूसरी उसी instant पे ले लेती है। कोई देना बिना लेने वाले के नहीं होता।
Chemists ने इस transaction को तीन lenses से देखा, हर एक पिछले से ज़्यादा powerful। Lens one सबसे पुराना है — classical view।
इसमें oxidation का मतलब है oxygen add करना या hydrogen हटाना, और reduction उसका एकदम उल्टा।
Magnesium को जलते हुए देखो: two magnesium plus oxygen देता है two magnesium oxide।
Magnesium में oxygen add हुआ, तो magnesium oxidise हुआ। अच्छा — पर यह lens तभी collapse हो जाता है जब reaction में oxygen और hydrogen बिल्कुल न हो।
तो idea को sharp करते हैं। Lens two कहता है असली event है electron transfer।
लो zinc plus copper two plus देता है zinc two plus plus copper। ना oxygen, ना hydrogen — फिर भी zinc दो electron खोता है और copper ion वो ले लेता है।
और यहीं से मिलता है chapter का सबसे famous mnemonic: <excited> O I L R I G — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain, electrons का।

sections.subtopic: Classical & Electronic Concepts and Oxidation Numbers
sections.title: The oxidation-number lens — and three cautions

board_events.text: Lens 3 — the oxidation-number (O.N.) view
In $CO_2$ electrons are shared, not transferred. So who lost and who gained?
O.N. = the hypothetical charge an atom would carry if each bond pair went to the more electronegative atom.
Oxidation = INCREASE in O.N.; Reduction = DECREASE in O.N.
Three cautions you must respect
(1) O.N. is not the real charge, and not the same as valency — valency has no sign, O.N. carries a sign and can be fractional.
(2) For a bond between two identical atoms (like an S–S link), the pair splits equally — zero contribution to each.
(3) A fractional O.N. is never a real per-atom charge — it is only an average; the structure reveals the truth.

segments.text: The electronic lens is powerful, but it too has a limit — and that limit forces us to invent something new.
Look at carbon dioxide. The electrons sit in covalent bonds, shared, not fully handed over. So who exactly lost and who gained? The clean electron-transfer story breaks down.

To keep a tidy ledger anyway, chemists invented the oxidation number. It is the hypothetical charge an atom would carry if every bonding pair were awarded entirely to the more electronegative atom. Pure book-keeping — but the single most useful tool in this chapter.
In this language the definitions become razor-sharp: oxidation is an increase in oxidation number, and reduction is a decrease. This works for any reaction, ionic or covalent.
Before we start computing, hold on to three cautions — examiners live in these gaps.
One: the oxidation number is not the real charge on the atom, and it is not valency. Valency is just a magnitude with no sign; oxidation number carries a sign and can even be fractional.
Two: when two identical atoms bond — say the sulphur to sulphur link in a polythionate — the shared pair is split equally, contributing zero to each.
Three, and this is the big one: <whisper> a fractional oxidation number is never a real charge on any single atom. It is only an average, and only the structure reveals the true per-atom values.
Electronic lens powerful है, पर इसकी भी एक limit है — और वही limit हमें कुछ नया invent करने पे मजबूर करती है।
Carbon dioxide देखो। Electrons covalent bonds में हैं, shared, पूरी तरह handed over नहीं। तो exactly किसने खोया और किसने पाया? Clean electron-transfer story यहाँ टूटती है।

फिर भी ledger tidy रखने के लिए, chemists ने oxidation number invent किया। यह वो hypothetical charge है जो atom पे होता अगर हर bonding pair ज़्यादा electronegative atom को पूरा दे दिया जाए। Pure book-keeping — पर इस chapter का सबसे useful tool।
इस language में definitions बिल्कुल sharp हो जाती हैं: oxidation मतलब oxidation number का increase, और reduction मतलब decrease। यह काम करता है किसी भी reaction पे, ionic या covalent।
Compute करने से पहले, तीन cautions याद रखो — examiners इन्हीं gaps में रहते हैं।
एक: oxidation number atom का real charge नहीं है, और valency भी नहीं। Valency सिर्फ एक magnitude है बिना sign के; oxidation number sign के साथ आता है और fractional भी हो सकता है।
दो: जब दो identical atoms bond करते हैं — जैसे polythionate में sulphur to sulphur link — shared pair बराबर split होती है, हर एक को zero contribution।
तीन, और यह सबसे बड़ा है: <whisper> fractional oxidation number कभी भी किसी single atom का real charge नहीं होता। यह सिर्फ average है, और सच सिर्फ structure बताता है।

sections.subtopic: Classical & Electronic Concepts and Oxidation Numbers
sections.title: Core definitions: oxidant, reductant, redox, disproportionation

board_events.text: The vocabulary that unlocks every problem
Oxidation: add O / remove H / lose electrons / increase in O.N.
Reduction: remove O / add H / gain electrons / decrease in O.N.
The agent does the OPPOSITE to itself.
Oxidising agent (oxidant): raises another's O.N.; it is itself REDUCED (gains electrons). E.g. $KMnO_4$, $K_2Cr_2O_7$, $HNO_3$.
Reducing agent (reductant): lowers another's O.N.; it is itself OXIDISED (loses electrons). E.g. active metals, $H_2S$, $I^-$.
Redox reaction: any reaction in which the O.N. of at least one element changes.
Disproportionation: the SAME element in one intermediate O.N. is simultaneously oxidised AND reduced.

segments.text: Now let's lock down the vocabulary, because half the marks in this chapter are won or lost on getting these labels the right way round.
Oxidation, said four equivalent ways: add oxygen, remove hydrogen, lose electrons, or increase the oxidation number. All the same event.
Reduction is its mirror: remove oxygen, add hydrogen, gain electrons, or decrease the oxidation number.
Here is the sentence that saves you every time: <whisper> the agent does the opposite to itself.
An oxidising agent raises another species' oxidation number, so it is itself reduced — it gains electrons. Think potassium permanganate, potassium dichromate, nitric acid.
A reducing agent lowers another's oxidation number, so it is itself oxidised — it loses electrons. Think active metals, hydrogen sulphide, the iodide ion.
A redox reaction is simply any reaction where the oxidation number of at least one element changes. That one check decides everything.
And a special one: disproportionation, where the same element sitting at a single intermediate oxidation number is oxidised and reduced at the same time. Hold that idea — it returns again and again.
अब vocabulary lock करते हैं, क्योंकि इस chapter के आधे marks इन्हीं labels के सही सीधे लगाने पे मिलते या जाते हैं।
Oxidation, चार equivalent तरीके से: oxygen add करो, hydrogen हटाओ, electrons खोओ, या oxidation number बढ़ाओ। सब एक ही event।
Reduction उसका mirror है: oxygen हटाओ, hydrogen add करो, electrons पाओ, या oxidation number घटाओ।
यह sentence हर बार बचाता है: <whisper> agent अपने आप के साथ उल्टा करता है।
Oxidising agent दूसरी species का oxidation number बढ़ाता है, तो खुद reduce होता है — electrons gain करता है। सोचो potassium permanganate, potassium dichromate, nitric acid।
Reducing agent दूसरे का oxidation number घटाता है, तो खुद oxidise होता है — electrons lose करता है। सोचो active metals, hydrogen sulphide, iodide ion।
Redox reaction simply वो है जहाँ कम से कम एक element का oxidation number change होता है। यह एक check सब decide कर देता है।
और एक special: disproportionation, जहाँ same element एक single intermediate oxidation number पे बैठा हुआ एक साथ oxidise और reduce होता है। इस idea को पकड़ो — यह बार बार वापस आएगा।

sections.title: The six assignment rules — and why each holds

board_events.text: Rules for assigning O.N. (with the reasoning)
1. Free element → 0. It has neither donated nor accepted anything — $S_8$, $P_4$, $O_3$ are all 0.
2. Monatomic ion → its charge. The hypothetical charge is the real charge; $Na^+ = +1$, $O^{2-} = -2$.
3. Fluorine is ALWAYS $-1$ in compounds — most electronegative, wins every pair.
4. Oxygen is usually $-2$. Exceptions: peroxide $-1$, superoxide $-\tfrac{1}{2}$, in $OF_2$ it is $+2$.
5. Hydrogen is usually $+1$. Exception: metal hydrides ($NaH$, $CaH_2$) give $-1$.
6. Charge-balance closes the system: $\sum$(O.N.) = net charge.
This single equation lets you solve for any one unknown O.N.

segments.text: These rules are not to be memorised blindly — each one has a reason, and the reason is what protects you when a formula tries to trick you.
Rule one: a free, uncombined element is always zero. It has neither donated nor accepted anything, so its ledger sits balanced at zero — sulphur in S eight, phosphorus in P four, ozone, all zero.
Rule two: a monatomic ion equals its own charge. There is nothing to share with, so the hypothetical charge is simply the real charge. Sodium plus one is plus one; oxide is minus two.
Rule three: fluorine is always minus one in compounds. It is the most electronegative element in existence, so it wins every bonding pair — no exceptions.

Rule four: oxygen is usually minus two, because it is second only to fluorine. The exceptions come only when oxygen bonds to itself or to fluorine: minus one in peroxides, minus one half in superoxides, and forced positive to plus two in oxygen difluoride.

Rule five: hydrogen is usually plus one, since it is less electronegative than most non-metals. But in metal hydrides like sodium hydride the metal is even weaker, so hydrogen wins and becomes minus one.
Rule six is the master closing rule: <curious> the signed oxidation numbers of all atoms must add up to the charge on the species.
For a neutral molecule that sum is zero; for an ion it is the ionic charge. This one equation is what lets you solve for any single unknown.
इन rules को blindly रट मत लगाओ — हर एक का एक reason है, और वही reason बचाता है जब कोई formula trick करने आता है।
Rule one: free, uncombined element हमेशा zero। उसने ना कुछ दिया ना लिया, तो ledger zero पे balanced बैठा है — S eight का sulphur, P four का phosphorus, ozone, सब zero।
Rule two: monatomic ion अपने charge के बराबर। Share करने को कुछ है ही नहीं, तो hypothetical charge simply real charge है। Sodium plus one है plus one; oxide minus two।
Rule three: fluorine compounds में हमेशा minus one। यह existence का सबसे electronegative element है, तो हर bonding pair जीत लेता है — no exceptions।

Rule four: oxygen usually minus two, क्योंकि यह fluorine के बाद दूसरा है। Exceptions तभी जब oxygen खुद से या fluorine से bond करे: peroxide में minus one, superoxide में minus one half, और oxygen difluoride में forced positive plus two।

Rule five: hydrogen usually plus one, क्योंकि यह ज़्यादातर non-metals से कम electronegative है। पर metal hydrides जैसे sodium hydride में metal और भी कमज़ोर है, तो hydrogen जीत के minus one बन जाता है।
Rule six master closing rule है: <curious> सारे atoms के signed oxidation numbers species के charge के बराबर add होने चाहिए।
Neutral molecule के लिए वो sum zero; ion के लिए ionic charge। यह एक equation ही किसी भी single unknown को solve करने देती है।

sections.subtopic: Classical & Electronic Concepts and Oxidation Numbers
sections.title: The master procedure & the peroxo trap (Caro's acid)

board_events.text: Solve for an unknown O.N. — five steps
Step 1: write the species and its net charge (neutral → 0; ion → its charge).
Step 2: plug in every known O.N. using the rules, times how many of each atom.
Step 3: let the unknown be $x$; write the charge-balance equation. Step 4: solve, watching signs.
Step 5: if the answer is fractional or busts the ceiling, check the structure.
The peroxo trap — $H_2SO_5$ (Caro's acid)
Blindly using $O = -2$ for all five oxygens gives $S = +8$ — impossible ($S$ maxes at $+6$).
The structure has ONE peroxide link: three O at $-2$, two O at $-1$ → returns the correct $S = +6$.

segments.text: Now the workflow itself — a five-step recipe you'll run dozens of times.
Step one: write down the species and its net charge. A neutral molecule sums to zero; an ion sums to its own charge.
Step two: plug in every oxidation number you already know from the rules, each multiplied by how many of that atom appear.
Step three: call the unknown x and write the charge-balance equation. Step four: solve it algebraically, and watch the signs like a hawk — this is where most marks quietly leak away.
Step five is the safety net: <whisper> if your answer comes out fractional or higher than the element can physically go, stop and check the structure.
Let me show you exactly why that fifth step matters, using Caro's acid, H two S O five.

Blindly taking all five oxygens as minus two gives sulphur plus eight. But sulphur can go no higher than plus six — so plus eight is chemically impossible. That is a red flag screaming that an assumption is wrong.

The structure reveals one peroxide linkage. Use three oxygens at minus two and two oxygens at minus one, and sulphur comes back to the correct plus six. The rule never failed — the blanket assumption did.
अब workflow खुद — एक five-step recipe जो तुम दर्जनों बार चलाओगे।
Step one: species और उसका net charge लिखो। Neutral molecule zero पे, ion अपने charge पे sum करता है।
Step two: जितने oxidation numbers rules से पहले से पता हैं सब plug करो, हर एक उस atom की count से multiply करके।
Step three: unknown को x बोलो और charge-balance equation लिखो। Step four: algebraically solve करो, और signs को बाज़ की तरह देखो — यहीं सबसे ज़्यादा marks चुपके से leak होते हैं।
Step five safety net है: <whisper> अगर answer fractional आए या element की physical ceiling से ऊपर चला जाए, रुक जाओ और structure check करो।
मैं दिखाता हूँ exactly क्यों यह पाँचवाँ step matter करता है, Caro's acid, H two S O five से।

Blindly सारे पाँच oxygen minus two लेने से sulphur plus eight आता है। पर sulphur plus six से ऊपर जा ही नहीं सकता — तो plus eight chemically impossible है। यह एक red flag है जो चीख रहा है कि कोई assumption गलत है।
Structure एक peroxide linkage दिखाता है। तीन oxygen minus two और दो oxygen minus one लो, और sulphur वापस correct plus six पे आ जाता है। Rule कभी fail नहीं हुआ — blanket assumption हुई।

sections.subtopic: Classical & Electronic Concepts and Oxidation Numbers
sections.title: The charge-balance master relation & the O.N. reference values

board_events.text: The one engine of this subtopic
Neutral molecule → sum is $0$; an ion → sum equals the ionic charge.
Usual O.N. values to memorise
O.N. is dimensionless, has no SI unit, and carries a sign.

segments.text: There is really only one equation in this subtopic, and everything else is convention feeding into it.
The master relation: the sum of the oxidation numbers over all atoms equals the net charge on the species.
For a neutral molecule that total is zero; for an ion it equals the ionic charge. That is the whole engine.
Around it sit the fixed values worth committing to memory, so you never re-derive the obvious ones under exam pressure.
Group one metals are plus one, group two are plus two, aluminium is plus three, and fluorine is always minus one.
Hydrogen is plus one — except in metal hydrides, where it flips to minus one.
Oxygen is minus two — except minus one in peroxides, minus one half in superoxides, plus two in oxygen difluoride, and plus one in dioxygen difluoride.
One last note on its nature: <curious> the oxidation number is a pure, dimensionless number with a sign. It has no S I unit — it is not a mass or a length, just a signed count.
इस subtopic में सच में सिर्फ एक equation है, बाकी सब convention उसमें feed करती है।
Master relation: सारे atoms के oxidation numbers का sum species के net charge के बराबर।
Neutral molecule के लिए total zero; ion के लिए ionic charge। यही पूरा engine है।
इसके around fixed values बैठे हैं जो याद रखने लायक हैं, ताकि exam pressure में obvious चीज़ें दोबारा derive ना करनी पड़े।
Group one metals plus one, group two plus two, aluminium plus three, और fluorine हमेशा minus one।
Hydrogen plus one — सिवाय metal hydrides के, जहाँ यह minus one हो जाता है।
Oxygen minus two — सिवाय peroxides में minus one, superoxides में minus one half, oxygen difluoride में plus two, और dioxygen difluoride में plus one।
इसकी nature पे एक आखिरी note: <curious> oxidation number एक pure, dimensionless number है sign के साथ। इसका कोई S I unit नहीं — यह mass या length नहीं, बस एक signed count है।

sections.subtopic: Classical & Electronic Concepts and Oxidation Numbers
sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): oxidant & reductant in $4Al + 3MnO_2$

board_events.text: Identify oxidised, reduced, oxidant, reductant
Assign O.N.: $Al$ (free) $= 0$; in $MnO_2$, $x + 2(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow Mn = +4$.
In $Al_2O_3$, $2x + 3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow Al = +3$; $Mn$ (free) $= 0$.
Track: $Al: 0 \rightarrow +3$ — increase → oxidised.
$Mn: +4 \rightarrow 0$ — decrease → reduced.
Al drives Mn's reduction → Al is the reductant; $MnO_2$ drives Al's oxidation → $MnO_2$ is the oxidant.
Answer: Al is oxidised (reducing agent); Mn in $MnO_2$ is reduced ($MnO_2$ is the oxidising agent).

segments.text: Let's run the machine on a clean C B S E board question: four aluminium plus three manganese dioxide gives two aluminium oxide plus three manganese.
Read the equation first, then assign oxidation numbers to the changing metals on both sides.
Aluminium on the left is a free element, so it is zero. In manganese dioxide, oxygen is minus two, so x plus two times minus two equals zero, giving manganese as plus four.
On the right, in aluminium oxide, two x plus three times minus two equals zero, giving aluminium plus three. And manganese on the right is a free element, so zero.
Now just track the movement. Aluminium goes from zero to plus three — that is an increase, so aluminium is oxidised.
Manganese goes from plus four to zero — a decrease, so manganese is reduced.

Finally name the agents, remembering the agent does the opposite to itself. Aluminium drives the reduction of manganese, so aluminium is the reducing agent; manganese dioxide drives the oxidation of aluminium, so it is the oxidising agent.
So the clean answer: aluminium is oxidised and is the reductant; the manganese in manganese dioxide is reduced, and manganese dioxide is the oxidant.
Machine को एक clean C B S E board question पे चलाते हैं: four aluminium plus three manganese dioxide देता है two aluminium oxide plus three manganese।
पहले equation पढ़ो, फिर दोनों side के changing metals को oxidation numbers assign करो।
Left पे aluminium free element है, तो zero। Manganese dioxide में oxygen minus two है, तो x plus two times minus two equals zero, मतलब manganese plus four।
Right पे, aluminium oxide में two x plus three times minus two equals zero, मतलब aluminium plus three। और right का manganese free element है, तो zero।
अब बस movement track करो। Aluminium zero से plus three — यह increase है, तो aluminium oxidise हुआ।
Manganese plus four से zero — decrease, तो manganese reduce हुआ।

अब agents name करो, याद रखते हुए कि agent अपने साथ उल्टा करता है। Aluminium manganese के reduction को drive करता है, तो aluminium reducing agent; manganese dioxide aluminium के oxidation को drive करता है, तो यह oxidising agent।
तो clean answer: aluminium oxidise हुआ और reductant है; manganese dioxide का manganese reduce हुआ, और manganese dioxide oxidant है।

sections.subtopic: Classical & Electronic Concepts and Oxidation Numbers
sections.title: Worked example (NEET speed trap): order chlorine's oxidation states

board_events.text: Arrange by increasing O.N. of chlorine
Species: $HCl,\ Cl_2,\ HClO,\ HClO_3,\ HClO_4$.
The trap: writing 'Cl = $-1$' everywhere. The moment Cl bonds to oxygen it is forced positive.
$Cl_2$: free element $\Rightarrow 0$.   $HCl$: $+1 + x = 0 \Rightarrow x = -1$.
$HClO$: $+1 + x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +1$.
$HClO_3$: $+1 + x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +5$.
$HClO_4$: $+1 + x - 8 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +7$.
Answer: $HCl(-1) \lt Cl_2(0) \lt HClO(+1) \lt HClO_3(+5) \lt HClO_4(+7)$.

segments.text: This is a N E E T speed trap — the whole point is to get the order in seconds, not to grind arithmetic.
You are asked to arrange five chlorine species by increasing oxidation number of chlorine: hydrochloric acid, chlorine gas, and the three oxoacids.
Here is the trap that catches the hurried student: <curious> reflexively writing chlorine as minus one everywhere. But the instant chlorine bonds to oxygen, it is forced positive.
Start with the easy anchors. Chlorine gas is a free element, so zero. In hydrochloric acid, hydrogen is plus one, so plus one plus x equals zero, giving x as minus one.
In hypochlorous acid, plus one plus x minus two equals zero, so chlorine is plus one.
In chloric acid, plus one plus x minus six equals zero, giving plus five.
In perchloric acid, plus one plus x minus eight equals zero, giving plus seven.

So the increasing order is: hydrochloric acid at minus one, then chlorine gas at zero, hypochlorous at plus one, chloric at plus five, and perchloric at plus seven. Notice the fast route — just watch the oxygen count climb in the oxoacids and the order fixes itself.
यह एक N E E T speed trap है — पूरा point है order seconds में निकालना, arithmetic घिसना नहीं।
तुमसे कहा गया है पाँच chlorine species को chlorine के बढ़ते oxidation number से arrange करो: hydrochloric acid, chlorine gas, और तीन oxoacids।
यह रहा वो trap जो जल्दबाज़ student को पकड़ता है: <curious> reflexively chlorine को हर जगह minus one लिखना। पर जैसे ही chlorine oxygen से bond करता है, वो forced positive हो जाता है।
आसान anchors से शुरू करो। Chlorine gas free element है, तो zero। Hydrochloric acid में hydrogen plus one, तो plus one plus x equals zero, x आया minus one।
Hypochlorous acid में plus one plus x minus two equals zero, तो chlorine plus one।
Chloric acid में plus one plus x minus six equals zero, तो plus five।
Perchloric acid में plus one plus x minus eight equals zero, तो plus seven।

तो बढ़ता order: hydrochloric acid minus one पे, फिर chlorine gas zero, hypochlorous plus one, chloric plus five, और perchloric plus seven। Fast route देखो — बस oxoacids में oxygen count चढ़ता देखो और order खुद fix हो जाता है।

segments.text: Now a J E E Main favourite that links oxidation-number assignment with structure and with redox behaviour — chromium pentoxide, C r O five.
A student computes chromium as plus ten. Watch the reasoning: taking all five oxygens as minus two gives x plus five times minus two equals zero, so x equals plus ten.

But here is the sanity check that must fire: <excited> chromium's maximum oxidation number is plus six, its group-based limit. Plus ten is chemically impossible — a red flag that the oxygen assignment is wrong.
Look at the real structure on the board. Chromium pentoxide has a butterfly shape: two side-on peroxide groups and one terminal doubly-bonded oxo oxygen.
That changes the bookkeeping completely. The two peroxide linkages give four oxygens at minus one, and the single oxo oxygen stays at minus two.
Redo the balance: x plus four times minus one plus one times minus two equals zero, so x minus six equals zero, and chromium comes out to plus six — exactly at its ceiling.
Now the bonus question they always attach. Since chromium is already at its highest accessible state, it cannot be oxidised any further; it can only be reduced.
So the answer is complete: chromium is correctly plus six, the plus ten error came from ignoring the peroxide linkages, and chromium pentoxide acts only as an oxidising agent.
अब एक J E E Main favourite जो oxidation-number assignment को structure और redox behaviour से जोड़ता है — chromium pentoxide, C r O five।
एक student chromium को plus ten निकालता है। Reasoning देखो: सारे पाँच oxygen minus two लेने से x plus five times minus two equals zero, तो x equals plus ten।
पर यहाँ यह sanity check fire होना चाहिए: <excited> chromium का maximum oxidation number plus six है, उसकी group-based limit। Plus ten chemically impossible है — red flag कि oxygen assignment गलत है।
Board पे असली structure देखो। Chromium pentoxide की butterfly shape है: दो side-on peroxide groups और एक terminal doubly-bonded oxo oxygen।
यह bookkeeping पूरी बदल देता है। दो peroxide linkages से चार oxygen minus one पे, और single oxo oxygen minus two पे रहता है।
Balance दोबारा: x plus four times minus one plus one times minus two equals zero, तो x minus six equals zero, और chromium आता है plus six — बिल्कुल अपनी ceiling पे।
अब वो bonus question जो हमेशा attach होता है। Chromium already अपने highest accessible state पे है, तो इसे और oxidise नहीं किया जा सकता; सिर्फ reduce।
तो answer complete: chromium correctly plus six, plus ten error peroxide linkages ignore करने से आया, और chromium pentoxide सिर्फ oxidising agent की तरह act करता है।

$+2.5$ is a WARNING, not a real charge — it is an average of unequal atoms.

board_events.text: Equal-split rule: an S–S bond divides its pair equally → zero contribution to each S.
Central S: bond only to other S → O.N. $= 0$ each.
Terminal S: like a sulphonate S (three O + one S) → O.N. $= +5$ each.

segments.text: Now the J E E Advanced level, where the fractional-average idea from earlier becomes the whole question — sodium tetrathionate.
First the naive average. With sodium plus one and oxygen minus two, two plus four x minus twelve equals zero, so four x is plus ten, and x is plus two point five.
That fraction is a warning, not an answer. Plus two point five is not a real charge on any sulphur — it is the average of unequal atoms.

So bring in the structure on the board. The tetrathionate ion is a chain of four sulphurs: two terminal sulphurs each carrying three oxygens, and two central sulphurs joined only by sulphur to sulphur bonds.
Now apply the equal-split rule for like atoms: a sulphur to sulphur bond divides its shared pair equally, contributing zero to each partner.
So the two central sulphurs bond only to other sulphurs, with no electronegative partner to lose electrons to — each central sulphur is exactly zero.
Each terminal sulphur sits like the sulphur in a sulphonate, bonded to three oxygens and one neutral-contribution sulphur, which works out to plus five each.

Verify against the average: two at plus five plus two at zero, all over four, is plus ten over four, which is plus two point five. <chuckle> It matches perfectly. So the honest answer is two terminal sulphurs at plus five and two central sulphurs at zero — the plus two point five was never a real per-atom value.
अब J E E Advanced level, जहाँ पहले वाला fractional-average idea पूरा question बन जाता है — sodium tetrathionate।
पहले naive average। Sodium plus one और oxygen minus two के साथ, two plus four x minus twelve equals zero, तो four x plus ten, और x plus two point five।
यह fraction एक warning है, answer नहीं। Plus two point five किसी भी sulphur का real charge नहीं — यह unequal atoms का average है।
तो board पे structure लाओ। Tetrathionate ion चार sulphur की chain है: दो terminal sulphur हर एक तीन oxygen carry करते, और दो central sulphur सिर्फ sulphur to sulphur bonds से जुड़े।
अब like atoms के लिए equal-split rule लगाओ: sulphur to sulphur bond अपनी shared pair बराबर बाँट देती है, हर partner को zero contribution।
तो दो central sulphur सिर्फ दूसरे sulphur से bond करते हैं, कोई electronegative partner नहीं जिसे electrons दे — हर central sulphur exactly zero।
हर terminal sulphur sulphonate के sulphur जैसा बैठा है, तीन oxygen और एक neutral-contribution sulphur से bonded, जो plus five each आता है।

Average से verify: दो plus five plus दो zero, सब four पे, plus ten over four, मतलब plus two point five। <chuckle> Perfectly match। तो honest answer: दो terminal sulphur plus five और दो central sulphur zero — plus two point five कभी real per-atom value था ही नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Classical & Electronic Concepts and Oxidation Numbers
sections.title: Pitfalls & pro-tips: signs, exception sweep, and the ceiling check

board_events.text: Where marks quietly disappear
Sign slips in charge-balance are the single biggest source of lost marks.
Forgetting O/H exceptions: applying $O = -2$ inside $H_2O_2$ or $H = +1$ inside $NaH$ gives nonsense.
Reading a fractional O.N. as physical reality — $+2.5$ in $S_4O_6^{2-}$ is an average, not any atom's charge.
Confusing the agent with what happens to it: the oxidising agent is the one that gets REDUCED.
Pro-tip: derive, don't memorise — but sweep first
Before computing, run a 3-second exception sweep for O–O, M–H, or O–F links.
Then check the ceiling: if your number busts the element's limit, you missed a peroxide — go to the structure.

segments.text: Let's close this subtopic with the traps examiners set on purpose, and the one habit that beats all of them.

The single biggest leak is a sign slip inside the charge-balance equation. Writing the wrong sign and then confidently solving turns a correct method into a wrong answer — slow down on the arithmetic.
Second, forgetting the oxygen and hydrogen exceptions. Applying minus two to the oxygen inside hydrogen peroxide, or plus one to the hydrogen inside sodium hydride, gives pure nonsense.
Third, reading a fractional oxidation number as if it were real. Plus two point five in tetrathionate is an average across unequal atoms, never a charge any single sulphur carries.
Fourth, the classic reversal: confusing the agent with what happens to it. Say it slowly — the oxidising agent is the one that gets reduced.
Now the pro-tip that ties it together. <whisper> Don't memorise oxidation-number tables — re-derive on the fly with the charge-balance rule.
But before you compute, run a three-second exception sweep of the formula, hunting for oxygen to oxygen, metal to hydrogen, or oxygen to fluorine links.

Then sanity-check against the element's allowed range — sulphur never exceeds plus six, nitrogen never exceeds plus five. If your number busts that ceiling, you missed a peroxide linkage, so go back to the structure.
इस subtopic को उन traps के साथ बंद करते हैं जो examiners जानबूझकर लगाते हैं, और वो एक habit जो सबको हराती है।
सबसे बड़ा leak charge-balance equation के अंदर sign slip है। गलत sign लिखकर confidently solve करना एक correct method को wrong answer बना देता है — arithmetic पे धीरे चलो।
दूसरा, oxygen और hydrogen exceptions भूलना। Hydrogen peroxide के oxygen को minus two, या sodium hydride के hydrogen को plus one लगाना pure nonsense देता है।
तीसरा, fractional oxidation number को real समझना। Tetrathionate का plus two point five unequal atoms का average है, कभी किसी single sulphur का charge नहीं।
चौथा, classic reversal: agent को उसके साथ होने वाली चीज़ से confuse करना। धीरे बोलो — oxidising agent वो है जो reduce होता है।
अब वो pro-tip जो सब जोड़ता है। <whisper> Oxidation-number tables रट मत लगाओ — charge-balance rule से on the fly re-derive करो।
पर compute करने से पहले, formula का तीन-second exception sweep चलाओ, ढूँढते हुए oxygen to oxygen, metal to hydrogen, या oxygen to fluorine links।
फिर element की allowed range से sanity-check करो — sulphur plus six से ऊपर नहीं, nitrogen plus five से ऊपर नहीं। अगर number ceiling तोड़ता है, तो peroxide linkage miss हुआ, structure पे वापस जाओ।

sections.subtopic: Balancing Redox Equations
sections.title: The two-account ledger and the electron see-saw

board_events.text: A balanced redox equation tallies TWO accounts
Mass: every atom on the left reappears on the right. Charge: total charge is identical on both sides.
The heart of it: electrons lost by the reductant = electrons gained by the oxidant, in the same instant.

board_events.text: Two bookkeeping systems (both correct)
1. Oxidation-number method: track total $\uparrow$ and $\downarrow$ in O.N., then scale so they match. Fast for molecular equations.
2. Half-reaction (ion-electron) method: split into two halves, balance each fully, equalise electrons, add. Cleaner for aqueous ionic reactions.
Both give the same answer — examiners specify which to use.

segments.text: Ordinary equations only have to balance atoms. Redox equations add a second demand — and that is exactly what makes them feel harder.

A balanced redox equation must tally two accounts at once. Mass: every atom that disappears from the left must reappear on the right. Charge: the total electrical charge must be identical on both sides.
And here is the single idea that unlocks all of it: electrons are never created or destroyed. Every electron lost by the reducing agent is gained, in the very same instant, by the oxidising agent.

Picture a see-saw with electrons as the children. The reductant's side rises because it has given electrons away; the oxidant's side drops because it has received them. The see-saw sits level only when electrons out equal electrons in.
To enforce that balance, chemists use two bookkeeping systems, and you should know both.

The first is the oxidation-number method: track how far each element's oxidation number goes up and down, then scale the species so the total increase equals the total decrease. It is fastest for molecular equations.

The second is the half-reaction, or ion-electron method: physically split the reaction into an oxidation half and a reduction half, balance each completely, make the electron counts equal, then add them back and cancel the electrons.

Both are correct and give the identical answer. <curious> The half-reaction method is usually cleaner for aqueous ionic reactions, while the oxidation-number method is faster for molecular ones — and examiners will tell you which they want.
Ordinary equations को सिर्फ atoms balance करने होते हैं। Redox equations एक दूसरी demand add करते हैं — और यही उन्हें मुश्किल feel कराता है।

एक balanced redox equation को एक साथ दो accounts tally करने होते हैं। Mass: हर atom जो left से गायब होता है वो right पे वापस आना चाहिए। Charge: total electrical charge दोनों side identical होना चाहिए।
और यह रहा वो single idea जो सब unlock करता है: electrons कभी create या destroy नहीं होते। Reducing agent द्वारा खोया हर electron उसी instant oxidising agent द्वारा gain होता है।

एक see-saw सोचो जिसमें electrons बच्चे हैं। Reductant की side ऊपर उठती है क्योंकि उसने electrons दिए; oxidant की side नीचे जाती है क्योंकि उसने लिए। See-saw तभी level बैठता है जब electrons out equal electrons in।
उस balance को enforce करने के लिए, chemists दो bookkeeping systems use करते हैं, और तुम्हें दोनों आने चाहिए।
पहला oxidation-number method: track करो हर element का oxidation number कितना ऊपर और नीचे गया, फिर species को scale करो ताकि total increase equal total decrease। Molecular equations के लिए सबसे fast।

दूसरा half-reaction, या ion-electron method: reaction को physically एक oxidation half और एक reduction half में split करो, हर एक को पूरा balance करो, electron counts equal करो, फिर वापस add करके electrons cancel करो।

दोनों correct हैं और identical answer देते हैं। <curious> Half-reaction method aqueous ionic reactions के लिए usually cleaner है, oxidation-number वाला molecular के लिए faster — और examiner बताएगा कौनसा चाहिए।

sections.subtopic: Balancing Redox Equations
sections.title: Limiting conditions & key definitions: medium is everything

board_events.text: Three things you must respect
(1) Medium matters: in ACID balance O and H with $H_2O$ and $H^+$; in BASE use $H_2O$ and $OH^-$. Mixing them is the top error.
(2) These methods assume an ionic (aqueous) reaction — convert a molecular equation to ionic form first.
(3) The product changes with medium: $MnO_4^-$ → $Mn^{2+}$ in acid (5 e$^-$) but → $MnO_2$ in neutral/mild base (3 e$^-$).
Definitions to carry forward
Half-reaction: one half alone — oxidation (electrons on the right) or reduction (electrons on the left).
Skeletal equation: the unbalanced reactant → product sketch. Spectator ions: unchanged ions, dropped in ionic form and restored later.
Electrons transferred $n$ = total O.N. change per formula unit — the SAME $n$ becomes the n-factor in titrations.

segments.text: Before we balance a single equation, three conditions must be respected — ignore any of them and the equation simply refuses to balance.

One, and the biggest: the medium matters. In acidic solution you balance oxygen and hydrogen with water and hydrogen ions; in basic solution you use water and hydroxide ions. Mixing the two is the single most common source of errors.
Two: these methods assume an ionic, aqueous reaction. If you are handed a molecular equation, convert it to ionic form first by dropping the spectator ions, balance, then convert back.

Three, and it catches even strong students: <whisper> the product itself changes with the medium. Permanganate goes to manganese two plus in acid, gaining five electrons, but only to manganese dioxide in neutral or mild base, gaining three. You cannot balance until you know the right product.
Now a few definitions we will lean on throughout.
A half-reaction is one half of the process written alone — the oxidation half has electrons on the product side, the reduction half has them on the reactant side.

The skeletal equation is the unbalanced reactant-to-product sketch you start from. Spectator ions are ions that never change — you drop them in ionic form and restore them only when converting back to molecular form.
And the number of electrons transferred, called n, equals the total oxidation-number change per formula unit. Remember this n — it returns as the n-factor when we do titrations in the next subtopic.
एक भी equation balance करने से पहले, तीन conditions respect करनी पड़ती हैं — किसी एक को ignore करो और equation balance करने से साफ मना कर देती है।

एक, और सबसे बड़ा: medium matters। Acidic solution में oxygen और hydrogen को water और hydrogen ions से balance करो; basic solution में water और hydroxide ions। दोनों को mix करना सबसे common error source है।
दो: यह methods ionic, aqueous reaction assume करते हैं। अगर molecular equation मिले, पहले spectator ions drop करके ionic form बनाओ, balance करो, फिर वापस convert करो।

तीन, और यह strong students को भी पकड़ता है: <whisper> product खुद medium के साथ बदलता है। Permanganate acid में manganese two plus जाता है, पाँच electrons gain करके, पर neutral या mild base में सिर्फ manganese dioxide, तीन gain करके। सही product जाने बिना balance नहीं कर सकते।
अब कुछ definitions जिनपे हम पूरे time टिक रहेंगे।
Half-reaction process का एक half अकेले लिखा हुआ है — oxidation half में electrons product side पे, reduction half में reactant side पे।

Skeletal equation वो unbalanced reactant-to-product sketch है जहाँ से शुरू करते हो। Spectator ions वो ions हैं जो कभी change नहीं होते — उन्हें ionic form में drop करो और सिर्फ molecular form में convert करते वक्त restore करो।
और transferred electrons की संख्या, जिसे n बोलते हैं, formula unit के total oxidation-number change के बराबर है। इस n को याद रखो — यह अगले subtopic के titrations में n-factor बनके वापस आएगा।

sections.subtopic: Balancing Redox Equations
sections.title: The oxidation-number method: five steps

board_events.text: Balance by tracking O.N. change
Step 1: assign O.N. to every atom and identify which elements change — you cannot balance electrons you haven't located.
Step 2: find the increase and decrease in O.N., per atom then per molecule (account for subscripts).
Step 3: make total increase = total decrease by multiplying oxidant and reductant by suitable integers.
This is the electron-balance principle in disguise: increase in O.N. is electrons lost; decrease is electrons gained.
Step 4: balance the remaining atoms by inspection, leaving H and O for last.
Step 5: balance O and H using the medium rules, then verify total charge.
Charge is the final, independent check that the electron bookkeeping was correct.

segments.text: The oxidation-number method works directly on the molecular or skeletal equation — no splitting required — in five steps.
Step one: assign an oxidation number to every atom and identify which elements actually change. The reasoning is blunt — you cannot balance electrons you have not yet located.

Step two: find the increase and the decrease in oxidation number, first per atom and then per molecule, carefully accounting for subscripts. A molecule may hold several atoms of the changing element, so the total change is what counts.
Step three is the core move: make the total increase equal the total decrease by multiplying the oxidant and reductant by suitable integers.
Why does that work? Because increase in oxidation number is just electrons lost, and decrease is electrons gained — this step is the electron-balance principle wearing a disguise.
Step four: balance the remaining atoms by inspection, but deliberately leave hydrogen and oxygen for last.
Step five: balance oxygen and hydrogen using the rules for the medium, then verify the total charge.
That final charge check is not optional. <curious> It is the independent test that your electron bookkeeping was actually correct — if the charges don't match, something upstream is wrong.
Oxidation-number method सीधे molecular या skeletal equation पे काम करता है — splitting की ज़रूरत नहीं — पाँच steps में।
Step one: हर atom को oxidation number assign करो और identify करो कौनसे elements सच में change होते हैं। Reasoning blunt है — तुम वो electrons balance नहीं कर सकते जो अभी तक locate नहीं किए।

Step two: oxidation number का increase और decrease निकालो, पहले per atom फिर per molecule, subscripts का ध्यान रखते हुए। एक molecule में changing element के कई atoms हो सकते हैं, तो total change matter करता है।
Step three core move है: total increase को total decrease के बराबर बनाओ, oxidant और reductant को suitable integers से multiply करके।
यह काम क्यों करता है? क्योंकि oxidation number का increase बस electrons lost है, और decrease electrons gained — यह step electron-balance principle का disguise है।
Step four: बाकी atoms को inspection से balance करो, पर hydrogen और oxygen को जानबूझकर last के लिए छोड़ो।
Step five: oxygen और hydrogen को medium के rules से balance करो, फिर total charge verify करो।
यह final charge check optional नहीं है। <curious> यह independent test है कि तुम्हारी electron bookkeeping सच में सही थी — अगर charges match ना करें, ऊपर कुछ गलत है।

sections.subtopic: Balancing Redox Equations
sections.title: The half-reaction method, the basic-medium shortcut, and back to molecular

board_events.text: Ion-electron method — six steps
Step 1: write the skeletal equation in ionic form (drop spectators). Step 2: split into oxidation and reduction halves.
Step 3: balance all atoms except O and H. Step 4: balance O with $H_2O$, then H with $H^+$ (acid) or $OH^-$ (base).
Step 5: balance charge by adding electrons to the more-positive side — those electrons are the n-factor of the half.
Step 6: multiply each half so electron counts match, add, cancel the electrons, and do a final atom-and-charge check.
The basic-medium shortcut (memorise this)
Balance the whole thing as if ACIDIC (using $H^+$); at the end add one $OH^-$ to BOTH sides for every $H^+$. The $H^+ + OH^-$ pairs collapse to $H_2O$; surplus waters cancel.
Back to molecular: re-attach the spectator ions you dropped, in the same numbers, to both sides — they never disturb a verified mass/charge balance.
Example: ionic $H_2S + 2Fe^{3+} \rightarrow 2H^+ + S + 2Fe^{2+}$ becomes $H_2S + 2FeCl_3 \rightarrow 2HCl + S + 2FeCl_2$.

segments.text: The half-reaction method is the cleaner route for aqueous ionic reactions. It runs in six steps.

Step one: write the skeletal equation in ionic form, dropping the spectator ions that only clutter the accounting. Step two: split it into an oxidation half and a reduction half so you can balance each cleanly.
Step three: in each half, balance every atom except oxygen and hydrogen. Step four: balance oxygen with water, then hydrogen with hydrogen ions in acid, or hydroxide ions in base.
Step five: balance the charge in each half by adding electrons to the more-positive side. Those electrons you add are precisely the n-factor of that half.
Step six: multiply each half so the electron counts match, add the halves, cancel the electrons, and finish with an atom-and-charge check.
Now the shortcut worth memorising, because it saves real time on basic-medium problems.

<excited> Balance the whole thing as if it were acidic, using hydrogen ions, and only at the very end add one hydroxide to both sides for every hydrogen ion. The hydrogen-ion and hydroxide pairs collapse into water, surplus waters cancel, and you are left with a correctly balanced basic equation.

Finally, to convert an ionic result back to molecular form, re-attach the spectator ions you dropped, in the same numbers, to both sides — because spectators never changed count, restoring them cannot disturb a balance you have already verified.

As a concrete example: the balanced ionic result for hydrogen sulphide with two iron three plus becomes the full molecular equation once the six spectator chloride ions are put back, giving hydrochloric acid and iron two chloride — no rebalancing needed.
Half-reaction method aqueous ionic reactions के लिए cleaner route है। यह छह steps में चलता है।

Step one: skeletal equation को ionic form में लिखो, उन spectator ions को drop करके जो सिर्फ accounting clutter करते हैं। Step two: इसे oxidation half और reduction half में split करो ताकि हर एक clean balance हो।
Step three: हर half में, oxygen और hydrogen के अलावा हर atom balance करो। Step four: oxygen को water से, फिर hydrogen को acid में hydrogen ions से, या base में hydroxide ions से balance करो।
Step five: हर half का charge balance करो, more-positive side पे electrons add करके। वो electrons जो तुम add करते हो, वही उस half का n-factor हैं।
Step six: हर half को multiply करो ताकि electron counts match करें, halves add करो, electrons cancel करो, और atom-and-charge check से finish करो।
अब वो shortcut जो याद रखने लायक है, क्योंकि यह basic-medium problems पे काफी time बचाता है।

<excited> पूरी चीज़ ऐसे balance करो जैसे acidic हो, hydrogen ions use करके, और सिर्फ एकदम end में हर hydrogen ion के लिए दोनों side एक hydroxide add करो। Hydrogen-ion और hydroxide pairs water में collapse हो जाते हैं, surplus waters cancel, और एक correctly balanced basic equation बच जाता है।

आखिर में, ionic result को वापस molecular form में convert करने के लिए, dropped spectator ions को same numbers में दोनों side re-attach करो — क्योंकि spectators ने count change नहीं किया, उन्हें restore करना already verified balance को disturb नहीं कर सकता।

एक concrete example: hydrogen sulphide और two iron three plus वाला balanced ionic result पूरा molecular equation बन जाता है जैसे ही छह spectator chloride ions वापस डाले जाते हैं, देते हुए hydrochloric acid और iron two chloride — बिना rebalancing।

sections.subtopic: Balancing Redox Equations
sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): balance $Cr_2O_7^{2-} + Sn^{2+}$ in acid

board_events.text: Ion-electron method, acidic medium
Reduction half ($Cr: +6 \rightarrow +3$):
Oxidation half ($Sn: +2 \rightarrow +4$): $Sn^{2+} \rightarrow Sn^{4+} + 2e^-$.
Equalise electrons: LCM of 6 and 2 is 6 → multiply the oxidation half by 3.
Charge check: left $-2 + 14 + 6 = +18$; right $+6 + 12 = +18$ ✓. Atoms balance ✓.

segments.text: Here is a textbook C B S E three-marker: balance dichromate reacting with tin two plus in acidic medium, by the ion-electron method.
Start from the skeletal ionic equation: dichromate plus tin two plus gives chromium three plus plus tin four plus.
Take the reduction half first — chromium falls from plus six to plus three.

Balanced, it reads: dichromate plus fourteen hydrogen ions plus six electrons gives two chromium three plus plus seven water. Two chromiums balance, seven oxygens go into seven waters, fourteen hydrogens into fourteen hydrogen ions, and the charge checks at plus six on both sides.
The oxidation half is simple: tin two plus gives tin four plus plus two electrons.
Now equalise the electrons. The reduction half releases six, the oxidation half two — their lowest common multiple is six, so multiply the oxidation half by three.
Add the two halves and cancel the six electrons: dichromate plus fourteen hydrogen ions plus three tin two plus gives two chromium three plus plus seven water plus three tin four plus.
Finish with the charge check. Left side is minus two plus fourteen plus six, which is plus eighteen; right side is plus six plus twelve, also plus eighteen. Charges match and atoms balance — done.
यह एक textbook C B S E three-marker है: dichromate को tin two plus के साथ acidic medium में balance करो, ion-electron method से।
Skeletal ionic equation से शुरू: dichromate plus tin two plus देता है chromium three plus plus tin four plus।
पहले reduction half लो — chromium plus six से plus three गिरता है।

Balanced, यह पढ़ता है: dichromate plus fourteen hydrogen ions plus six electrons देता है two chromium three plus plus seven water। दो chromium balance, सात oxygen सात water में, fourteen hydrogen fourteen hydrogen ions में, और charge दोनों side plus six पे check होता है।
Oxidation half simple है: tin two plus देता है tin four plus plus two electrons।
अब electrons equalise करो। Reduction half छह release करता है, oxidation half दो — उनका lowest common multiple छह है, तो oxidation half को तीन से multiply करो।
दोनों halves add करके छह electrons cancel करो: dichromate plus fourteen hydrogen ions plus three tin two plus देता है two chromium three plus plus seven water plus three tin four plus।
Charge check से finish। Left side minus two plus fourteen plus six, मतलब plus eighteen; right side plus six plus twelve, भी plus eighteen। Charges match और atoms balance — हो गया।

sections.subtopic: Balancing Redox Equations
sections.title: Worked example (NEET speed trap): the coefficient of $H^+$

board_events.text: Find only the $H^+$ coefficient — don't balance everything
Electrons first: $Mn: +7 \rightarrow +2$ gains 5 e$^-$; each C in oxalate $+3 \rightarrow +4$, and there are 2 C → loses 2 e$^-$.
LCM $= 10 \Rightarrow$ 2 $MnO_4^-$ and 5 $C_2O_4^{2-}$.
Speed logic for H: total O on left $= 2(4) + 5(4) = 28$; 10 $CO_2$ hold 20, so 8 O go into 8 $H_2O$ → 16 $H^+$.
Answer: 16. Traps: writing 5 oxalate → 5 $CO_2$ (it's 10), or counting oxalate as a 1-electron donor (it's 2).
For 'find the coefficient' questions, never balance the whole equation — count electrons, take the LCM, and read it off.

segments.text: This is a N E E T speed trap, and the discipline it teaches is priceless: <whisper> when they ask for one coefficient, never balance the whole equation.
The reaction is permanganate plus oxalate in acid, giving manganese two plus and carbon dioxide. We only want the coefficient of the hydrogen ion.

So count electrons first. Manganese falls from plus seven to plus two, gaining five electrons per permanganate. In oxalate, each carbon rises from plus three to plus four, and there are two carbons, so oxalate loses two electrons.
Balance those electrons with the lowest common multiple, ten. That means two permanganates gaining ten electrons and five oxalates losing ten.
The balanced line is two permanganate plus five oxalate plus sixteen hydrogen ions gives two manganese two plus plus ten carbon dioxide plus eight water.

Here is the fast way to the hydrogen without full balancing. Total oxygen on the left is two times four plus five times four, which is twenty-eight. Ten carbon dioxide molecules hold twenty of those, so the remaining eight oxygens go into eight waters, which demands sixteen hydrogen ions.

So the answer is sixteen. Watch the two traps: writing five oxalate to five carbon dioxide when it is actually ten, since each oxalate has two carbons; and treating oxalate as a one-electron donor when it is a two-electron donor.

Bank the habit for these questions — get the electron count from the oxidation-number changes, take the lowest common multiple to fix the two main reactants, then balance oxygen with water and hydrogen with hydrogen ions, and the coefficient you want falls out in about two lines.
यह एक N E E T speed trap है, और जो discipline यह सिखाता है वो priceless है: <whisper> जब एक coefficient पूछें, कभी पूरी equation balance मत करो।
Reaction है permanganate plus oxalate acid में, देता है manganese two plus और carbon dioxide। हमें सिर्फ hydrogen ion का coefficient चाहिए।

तो पहले electrons count करो। Manganese plus seven से plus two गिरता है, per permanganate पाँच electrons gain करता है। Oxalate में हर carbon plus three से plus four चढ़ता है, और दो carbons हैं, तो oxalate दो electrons lose करता है।
उन electrons को lowest common multiple, दस, से balance करो। मतलब दो permanganate दस electrons gain करते, और पाँच oxalate दस lose करते।
Balanced line: two permanganate plus five oxalate plus sixteen hydrogen ions देता है two manganese two plus plus ten carbon dioxide plus eight water।

यह रहा hydrogen तक पहुँचने का fast तरीका बिना full balancing। Left पे total oxygen दो times four plus five times four, मतलब twenty-eight। दस carbon dioxide molecules बीस hold करते हैं, तो बाकी आठ oxygen आठ water में जाते हैं, जो sixteen hydrogen ions माँगता है।

तो answer sixteen। दो traps देखो: पाँच oxalate को पाँच carbon dioxide लिखना जबकि वो actually दस है, क्योंकि हर oxalate में दो carbon; और oxalate को one-electron donor मानना जबकि वो two-electron donor है।

इन questions के लिए habit bank कर लो — electron count oxidation-number changes से लो, lowest common multiple से दो main reactants fix करो, फिर oxygen को water और hydrogen को hydrogen ions से balance करो, और जो coefficient चाहिए वो दो line में आ जाता है।

sections.subtopic: Balancing Redox Equations
sections.title: Worked example (JEE Main): balance $MnO_4^- + I^-$ in BASIC medium

board_events.text: Ion-electron method, basic medium
Reduction half ($Mn: +7 \rightarrow +4$, gains 3 e$^-$):
Oxidation half: $2I^- \rightarrow I_2 + 2e^-$. Equalise (LCM $6$): reduction $\times 2$, oxidation $\times 3$.
Charge check: left $-2 - 6 = -8$; right $-8$ ✓. Note $MnO_4^-$ takes only 3 e$^-$ here, not 5 — the medium set the product.

segments.text: Now a J E E Main problem that forces the basic-medium rules to fire — permanganate oxidising iodide to iodine, with manganese landing at manganese dioxide.
The skeletal reaction is permanganate plus iodide gives manganese dioxide plus iodine. Notice immediately that the product is manganese dioxide, not manganese two plus, because the medium is basic.

Take the reduction half. Manganese falls from plus seven to plus four, gaining three electrons. Balanced for base, it reads permanganate plus two water plus three electrons gives manganese dioxide plus four hydroxide. Check it: six oxygens each side, four hydrogens each side, and charge minus four each side.
The oxidation half is two iodide gives iodine plus two electrons.
Equalise the electrons at their lowest common multiple, six — multiply the reduction half by two and the oxidation half by three.
The doubled reduction half is two permanganate plus four water plus six electrons gives two manganese dioxide plus eight hydroxide.
Add the halves and cancel the six electrons: two permanganate plus six iodide plus four water gives two manganese dioxide plus three iodine plus eight hydroxide.

Charge check closes it: left is minus two minus six, which is minus eight; right is minus eight. <curious> And note the lesson — here permanganate accepts only three electrons, not five, purely because the basic medium set a different product.
अब एक J E E Main problem जो basic-medium rules को fire करने पे मजबूर करता है — permanganate iodide को iodine में oxidise करता है, manganese manganese dioxide पे land करता है।
Skeletal reaction: permanganate plus iodide देता है manganese dioxide plus iodine। तुरंत notice करो कि product manganese dioxide है, manganese two plus नहीं, क्योंकि medium basic है।

Reduction half लो। Manganese plus seven से plus four गिरता है, तीन electrons gain करके। Base के लिए balanced, यह पढ़ता है permanganate plus two water plus three electrons देता है manganese dioxide plus four hydroxide। Check करो: छह oxygen हर side, चार hydrogen हर side, और charge minus four हर side।
Oxidation half: two iodide देता है iodine plus two electrons।
Electrons को उनके lowest common multiple, छह, पे equalise करो — reduction half को two से और oxidation half को three से multiply करो।
Doubled reduction half: two permanganate plus four water plus six electrons देता है two manganese dioxide plus eight hydroxide।
Halves add करके छह electrons cancel करो: two permanganate plus six iodide plus four water देता है two manganese dioxide plus three iodine plus eight hydroxide।

Charge check बंद करता है: left minus two minus six, मतलब minus eight; right minus eight। <curious> और lesson notice करो — यहाँ permanganate सिर्फ तीन electrons लेता है, पाँच नहीं, सिर्फ इसलिए कि basic medium ने अलग product set किया।

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Advanced): $P_4 + OH^-$ disproportionation

board_events.text: White phosphorus with hot NaOH — classify and balance
Classify: $P$ in $P_4 = 0$; in $PH_3$ it is $-3$ (reduced); in $H_2PO_2^-$ it is $+1$ (oxidised) → disproportionation.
Reduction needs 3 e$^-$ (0 → $-3$); oxidation releases 1 e$^-$ (0 → $+1$) → 1 P reduced per 3 P oxidised.

Check: O left $3 + 3 = 6$, right $6$ ✓; H left $3 + 6 = 9$, right $3 + 6 = 9$ ✓; charge $-3$ each side ✓.

segments.text: The J E E Advanced problem combines classification with basic-medium balancing — white phosphorus reacting with hot sodium hydroxide.
The skeleton is phosphorus four plus hydroxide gives phosphine plus hypophosphite. Classify before you balance.

Phosphorus in P four is zero. In phosphine it is minus three, so it is reduced; in hypophosphite it is plus one, so it is oxidised. The same element, from one starting state, ends up both lower and higher — this is a disproportionation.

Now the electron bookkeeping per atom. Reduction from zero to minus three needs three electrons; oxidation from zero to plus one releases one electron. To balance electrons, one phosphorus must be reduced for every three that are oxidised.
The board shows this split clearly: one P four molecule branches into a reduction path making phosphine and an oxidation path making hypophosphite, with one phosphorus reduced per three oxidised.

So of the four phosphorus atoms in P four, one goes to phosphine and three go to hypophosphite. The skeleton becomes P four gives phosphine plus three hypophosphite, and the phosphorus atoms already balance.
Now balance oxygen, hydrogen and charge in base. The result is P four plus three hydroxide plus three water gives phosphine plus three hypophosphite.

Verify all three accounts: oxygen is six on each side, hydrogen is nine on each side, and the charge is minus three on each side. <excited> Everything ties out — a genuine disproportionation, balanced end to end.
J E E Advanced problem classification को basic-medium balancing से जोड़ता है — white phosphorus hot sodium hydroxide के साथ react करता है।
Skeleton है phosphorus four plus hydroxide देता है phosphine plus hypophosphite। Balance करने से पहले classify करो।

P four में phosphorus zero है। Phosphine में minus three, तो reduced; hypophosphite में plus one, तो oxidised। Same element, एक starting state से, दोनों lower और higher पे खत्म — यह disproportionation है।

अब per atom electron bookkeeping। Zero से minus three reduction को तीन electrons चाहिए; zero से plus one oxidation एक electron release करता है। Electrons balance करने को, हर तीन oxidise होने वाले phosphorus पे एक reduce होना चाहिए।
Board यह split साफ दिखाता है: एक P four molecule एक reduction path में phosphine बनाती और एक oxidation path में hypophosphite, एक phosphorus reduced per तीन oxidised।
तो P four के चार phosphorus atoms में से, एक phosphine जाता है और तीन hypophosphite। Skeleton बनता है P four देता है phosphine plus three hypophosphite, और phosphorus atoms already balance।
अब base में oxygen, hydrogen और charge balance करो। Result: P four plus three hydroxide plus three water देता है phosphine plus three hypophosphite।
तीनों accounts verify करो: oxygen हर side छह, hydrogen हर side नौ, और charge हर side minus three। <excited> सब tie out — एक genuine disproportionation, end to end balanced।

sections.subtopic: Balancing Redox Equations
sections.title: Pitfalls & pro-tips: charge check, medium, and equalising electrons

board_events.text: The four balancing traps
Balancing atoms but forgetting charge — an equation can have every atom matched and still be wrong. Always finish with a charge check.
Using the wrong medium's ions — putting $H^+$ in a basic answer (or vice-versa) is the number-one examiner trap. Decide the medium before balancing H and O.
Adding halves without equalising electrons — if one half releases 3 e$^-$ and the other absorbs 2, scale to a common 6 first, or electrons survive in the final equation.
Assuming a fixed product regardless of medium — wrong product means wrong electron count means everything downstream fails.
Pro-tip: coefficients fast, base via acid
For 'find the coefficient of X', get the electron count from O.N. changes, take the LCM to fix the two reactants, then balance O and H — the answer falls out in two lines.
For any basic-medium problem, balance it as acidic first, then add $OH^-$ to both sides to mop up every $H^+$.

segments.text: Let's close balancing with the four traps that cost the most marks, then the two habits that neutralise them.

First: balancing atoms but forgetting charge. An equation can have every atom matched and still be wrong, because the charge does not tally. Always finish with a charge check — it catches almost every slip.

Second, and the number-one examiner trap: using the wrong medium's ions. Putting hydrogen ions into a basic-medium answer, or hydroxide into an acidic one, is the classic error. Decide the medium before you touch hydrogen and oxygen.

Third: adding the two halves without equalising electrons. If one half releases three electrons and the other absorbs two, you must scale both to a common six before adding — otherwise leftover electrons survive in your final equation.
Fourth: assuming a fixed product regardless of medium. Permanganate does not always become manganese two plus. A wrong product gives a wrong electron count, and everything downstream collapses.
Now the pro-tips. For any question asking only for the coefficient of one species, don't balance the whole thing.

Get the electron count from the oxidation-number changes, take the lowest common multiple to fix the two main reactants, then balance oxygen with water and hydrogen with the medium's ions — the coefficient you want usually appears in two lines.

And for any basic-medium problem: <whisper> balance it as acidic first, then add one hydroxide to both sides for every hydrogen ion to mop them up. Far fewer mistakes than balancing in base from scratch.
Balancing को उन चार traps के साथ बंद करते हैं जो सबसे ज़्यादा marks खा जाते हैं, फिर वो दो habits जो उन्हें neutralise करती हैं।
पहला: atoms balance करना पर charge भूलना। एक equation में हर atom match हो सकता है और फिर भी गलत हो, क्योंकि charge tally नहीं करता। हमेशा charge check से finish करो — यह लगभग हर slip पकड़ता है।

दूसरा, और number-one examiner trap: गलत medium के ions use करना। Basic-medium answer में hydrogen ions डालना, या acidic में hydroxide, classic error है। Hydrogen और oxygen को हाथ लगाने से पहले medium decide करो।

तीसरा: दो halves को electrons equalise किए बिना add करना। अगर एक half तीन electrons release करे और दूसरा दो absorb, दोनों को common छह पे scale करो add करने से पहले — वरना बचे electrons final equation में survive कर जाते हैं।
चौथा: medium के बावजूद fixed product मानना। Permanganate हमेशा manganese two plus नहीं बनता। गलत product गलत electron count देता है, और पूरा downstream collapse हो जाता है।
अब pro-tips। किसी भी question में जो सिर्फ एक species का coefficient माँगे, पूरी चीज़ balance मत करो।

Electron count oxidation-number changes से लो, lowest common multiple से दो main reactants fix करो, फिर oxygen को water और hydrogen को medium के ions से balance करो — जो coefficient चाहिए वो usually दो line में आ जाता है।

और किसी भी basic-medium problem के लिए: <whisper> इसे पहले acidic ऐसे balance करो, फिर हर hydrogen ion के लिए दोनों side एक hydroxide add करके उन्हें mop up करो। Base में scratch से balance करने से काफी कम गलतियाँ।

sections.subtopic: Redox Titrations & Electrochemical Cells
sections.title: Two faces of a balanced redox reaction: measuring and making electricity

board_events.text: Two powerful things you can do with a redox reaction
Face 1 — the redox titration: a chemical weighing-scale where the 'weights' are electrons.
Run a known oxidant (e.g. $KMnO_4$) into an unknown reductant until every electron it can give is taken — the endpoint.
$KMnO_4$ is self-indicating: the first excess drop turns the flask permanent pink.
Face 2 — the galvanic (voltaic) cell: separate the two halves so electrons must travel through a wire, capturing the flow as current.
Oxidation happens at the anode (electrons released); reduction at the cathode (electrons consumed).
Mnemonic: An Ox / Red Cat — Anode = Oxidation, Reduction = Cathode. Electrons flow anode → cathode in the wire.
The salt bridge is the quiet hero: its ions keep each beaker neutral, without which the electron flow chokes.

segments.text: You already know how to balance a redox reaction. This subtopic is about two powerful things you can then do with one: measure with it, and harvest electricity from it.
The first face is the redox titration — think of a taraazu, the two-pan balance a vegetable seller uses, except here the weights are electrons.

You run a known oxidant, say potassium permanganate, from a burette into an unknown reductant until every electron the reductant can give has been taken. That instant is the endpoint, where equal numbers of electrons — equal equivalents — have been exchanged.
Permanganate has a lovely bonus: <curious> it is self-indicating. The moment one drop goes unreacted, the whole solution turns permanent pink, so you need no separate indicator.

The second face is the galvanic cell. If zinc simply touches copper sulphate, the electrons jump directly and the energy escapes as heat. But separate the two halves into two beakers and force the electrons through a wire, and you capture that flow as electric current — like channelling a waterfall through a turbine.
Inside the cell, oxidation and reduction happen in different rooms. The room releasing electrons is the anode; the room consuming them is the cathode.
Remember it as An Ox, Red Cat: anode is oxidation, reduction is cathode. And electrons always march through the external wire from anode to cathode, never through the solution.
One piece is easy to forget: the salt bridge. Its ions trickle across to keep each beaker electrically neutral — without it, the charge imbalance would choke the electron flow within seconds.
तुम्हें पहले से आता है redox reaction balance करना। यह subtopic उन दो powerful चीज़ों के बारे में है जो तुम फिर एक reaction से कर सकते हो: उससे measure करना, और उससे electricity harvest करना।
पहला face है redox titration — एक तराज़ू सोचो जो sabziwala use करता है, बस यहाँ weights electrons हैं।

तुम एक known oxidant, जैसे potassium permanganate, burette से unknown reductant में चलाते हो जब तक reductant का हर electron ले न लिया जाए। वो instant endpoint है, जहाँ बराबर electrons — बराबर equivalents — exchange हुए हैं।
Permanganate का एक प्यारा bonus है: <curious> यह self-indicating है। जैसे ही एक drop unreacted जाता है, पूरा solution permanent pink हो जाता है, तो अलग indicator चाहिए ही नहीं।

दूसरा face है galvanic cell। अगर zinc सीधे copper sulphate को छू ले, electrons directly कूद जाते हैं और energy heat की तरह बर्बाद हो जाती है। पर दोनों halves को दो beakers में अलग करो और electrons को wire से गुज़ारो, तो वो flow electric current बन जाता है — जैसे waterfall को turbine से channel करना।
Cell के अंदर, oxidation और reduction अलग rooms में होते हैं। जो room electrons release करता है वो anode; जो consume करता है वो cathode।
इसे याद रखो An Ox, Red Cat: anode is oxidation, reduction is cathode। और electrons हमेशा external wire से anode से cathode जाते हैं, solution से कभी नहीं।
एक हिस्सा भूलना आसान है: salt bridge। इसके ions दोनों beakers को electrically neutral रखते हैं — इसके बिना charge imbalance seconds में electron flow को choke कर देता।

sections.subtopic: Redox Titrations & Electrochemical Cells
sections.title: Definitions & limiting conditions: electrode potential, cell notation, spontaneity

board_events.text: Key definitions for cells
Electrode potential $E$: the tendency of a half-cell to gain electrons (be reduced). At 1 M ions, 1 bar, 298 K it is the standard value $E^\circ$ (a reduction potential, by IUPAC convention).
Cell notation: anode $\mid$ anode soln $\parallel$ cathode soln $\mid$ cathode (oxidation written on the left).
Three limiting conditions
(1) A titration needs a sharp endpoint and the right medium — $KMnO_4$ is titrated in dilute $H_2SO_4$, never $HCl$ (which it would also oxidise).
(2) A galvanic cell runs spontaneously only when $E^\circ_{cell} \gt 0$ (equivalently $\Delta G \lt 0$); a negative EMF means the reaction runs the other way.
(3) Standard $E^\circ$ values assume 1 M ions, 1 bar gases, 298 K — change the concentrations and the actual EMF shifts (the Nernst correction).
Electrons flow toward the species that craves them most; the salt bridge keeps the circuit alive.

segments.text: Before the formulas, fix the definitions and the conditions under which they apply.

The electrode potential, written E, is the tendency of a half-cell to gain electrons — that is, to be reduced. Measured at one molar ions, one bar, and two hundred ninety-eight kelvin, it becomes the standard electrode potential, E standard, and by I U P A C convention it is always reported as a reduction potential.
Cell notation writes the anode on the left and the cathode on the right, with a single line for a phase boundary and a double line for the salt bridge. Oxidation on the left, reduction on the right.
Now three conditions that decide whether any of this works.

One: a titration needs a sharp, detectable endpoint and the right medium. Permanganate is titrated in dilute sulphuric acid, never hydrochloric — because permanganate would also oxidise the chloride, consuming extra titrant and ruining the result.

Two: a galvanic cell runs spontaneously only when the standard cell E M F is greater than zero, which is the same as saying the Gibbs free energy change is negative. If you compute a negative E M F, the reaction actually runs the other way.

Three: the clean standard values assume standard conditions — one molar ions, one bar gases, two hundred ninety-eight kelvin. Change the concentrations and the real E M F shifts, and that correction is the Nernst equation, which we will meet shortly.
The unifying picture: electrons flow toward whichever species craves them most, and the salt bridge quietly keeps the whole circuit alive.
Formulas से पहले, definitions और वो conditions fix कर लो जिनके तहत यह लागू होते हैं।

Electrode potential, जिसे E लिखते हैं, एक half-cell की tendency है electrons gain करने की — यानी reduce होने की। One molar ions, one bar, दो सौ अठानवे kelvin पे यह standard electrode potential, E standard बन जाता है, और I U P A C convention से हमेशा reduction potential की तरह report होता है।
Cell notation anode को left पे और cathode को right पे लिखता है, phase boundary के लिए single line और salt bridge के लिए double line। Oxidation left पे, reduction right पे।
अब तीन conditions जो decide करती हैं कि यह सब काम करेगा या नहीं।

एक: titration को sharp, detectable endpoint और सही medium चाहिए। Permanganate dilute sulphuric acid में titrate होता है, hydrochloric में कभी नहीं — क्योंकि permanganate chloride को भी oxidise कर देता, extra titrant consume करके result बिगाड़ देता।

दो: galvanic cell तभी spontaneously चलता है जब standard cell E M F zero से बड़ा हो, जो वही बात है कि Gibbs free energy change negative हो। अगर negative E M F निकले, reaction actually उल्टी दिशा में चलती है।

तीन: clean standard values standard conditions assume करती हैं — one molar ions, one bar gases, दो सौ अठानवे kelvin। Concentrations बदलो और real E M F shift हो जाता है, और वो correction Nernst equation है, जो जल्दी मिलेगी।
Unifying picture: <curious> electrons उस species की तरफ बहते हैं जो उन्हें सबसे ज़्यादा चाहती है, और salt bridge चुपचाप पूरे circuit को alive रखता है।
