board_events.text: Step 1: identify each species' n-factor from its O.N. change in that medium (the medium fixes the product, so it fixes n).
Step 2: write the endpoint balance $\text{meq}_{ox} = \text{meq}_{red}$, i.e. $M_1 n_1 V_1 = M_2 n_2 V_2$.
At the endpoint, electrons given exactly equal electrons taken — so equivalents must match, never raw moles.
Step 3: substitute the three known quantities and solve for the fourth, keeping volumes in the same unit.
Step 4: sanity-check the magnitude — a higher n-factor reagent needs proportionally less volume.
This single balance, equivalents in equals equivalents out, is all a titration ever asks.

segments.text: Here is the procedure for any redox titration — just four steps.
Picture the setup on the board: the known oxidant, permanganate, drips from the burette into the unknown reductant in the flask, and the flask turns pink exactly at the endpoint.

Step one: identify each species' n-factor from its oxidation-number change in that medium. This matters because the medium fixes the product — permanganate takes five electrons in acid but three in neutral — and the product fixes the n-factor.
Step two: write the endpoint balance. Milliequivalents of oxidant equal milliequivalents of reductant, which in symbols is M one n one V one equals M two n two V two.

Why equivalents and not moles? Because at the endpoint the electrons given exactly equal the electrons taken, and equivalents — moles times n-factor — are what count electrons. Matching raw moles would ignore how many electrons each species carries.
Step three: substitute the three quantities you know and solve for the fourth, keeping all volumes in the same unit throughout.
Step four: sanity-check the size of your answer. A reagent with a higher n-factor delivers more electrons per mole, so it needs proportionally less volume.
That is the whole game — equivalents in equals equivalents out, and the unknown falls out of one line.
यह रहा किसी भी redox titration का procedure — सिर्फ चार steps।
Board पे setup देखो: known oxidant, permanganate, burette से flask में unknown reductant में drip होता है, और flask exactly endpoint पे pink हो जाता है।

Step one: हर species का n-factor उसके oxidation-number change से पहचानो, उस medium में। यह matter करता है क्योंकि medium product fix करता है — permanganate acid में पाँच electrons लेता है पर neutral में तीन — और product n-factor fix करता है।
Step two: endpoint balance लिखो। Milliequivalents of oxidant equal milliequivalents of reductant, जो symbols में M one n one V one equals M two n two V two है।

Equivalents क्यों, moles क्यों नहीं? क्योंकि endpoint पे electrons given exactly electrons taken के बराबर होते हैं, और equivalents — moles times n-factor — electrons count करते हैं। Raw moles match करना ignore कर देता कि हर species कितने electrons carry करती है।
Step three: जो तीन quantities पता हैं substitute करो और चौथी solve करो, सारे volumes एक ही unit में रखते हुए।
Step four: अपने answer के size की sanity-check करो। ज़्यादा n-factor वाला reagent per mole ज़्यादा electrons देता है, तो उसे proportionally कम volume चाहिए।
यही पूरा game है — equivalents in equal equivalents out, और unknown एक line में निकल आता है।

sections.subtopic: Redox Titrations & Electrochemical Cells
sections.title: Procedure B: building a galvanic cell, and why $E^\circ$ chooses your titrant

board_events.text: Predict / build a galvanic cell
Step 1: list both half-reactions as reductions with their $E^\circ$. Step 2: the higher-$E^\circ$ half-cell is the cathode; the lower-$E^\circ$ one is the anode (its sign reverses on oxidation).
Step 3: $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$; a positive value confirms spontaneity. Step 4: find $n$ = total electrons in the BALANCED cell reaction (not per atom).
Step 5: link to feasibility via $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell}$ and, if needed, $\log K = nE^\circ_{cell}/0.0591$.
Activity-series shortcut: a metal displaces the ion of any metal below it — Zn ($-0.76$ V) displaces Cu ($+0.34$ V), but Cu cannot displace Zn.
$E^\circ$ explains the titration too
An oxidant can titrate a reductant only if $E^\circ_{cell} \gt 0$.
$MnO_4^-$ ($+1.51$ V) and $Cr_2O_7^{2-}$ ($+1.33$ V) sit above common reductants like $Fe^{2+}$ ($+0.77$ V), so their titrations run to completion.
The $HCl$ problem, from potentials: $Cl_2/Cl^-$ is $+1.36$ V — below $MnO_4^-$ (so permanganate oxidises chloride) but above dichromate (so dichromate tolerates $HCl$).

segments.text: Now the mirror procedure — predicting or building a galvanic cell.

Step one: list both half-reactions as reductions with their standard potentials. Step two: the half-cell with the higher potential becomes the cathode, because it pulls electrons harder, so reduction wins there; the lower-potential half-cell is forced into oxidation and becomes the anode, its sign reversing.

Step three: the cell E M F is the cathode potential minus the anode potential, and a positive value confirms the cell is spontaneous as written. Step four, and the most common slip: n is the total electrons exchanged in the balanced cell reaction, not the number per atom.

Step five: link to energy and feasibility. The standard Gibbs free energy change is minus n F times the cell E M F, and if you need the equilibrium constant, log K equals n times the cell E M F divided by zero point zero five nine one.

There is a fast shortcut hiding here — the activity series. A metal displaces the ion of any metal below it. Zinc, at minus zero point seven six volts, displaces copper at plus zero point three four; but a copper spoon in zinc nitrate does nothing.
And here is a beautiful connection: <curious> the electrode-potential idea is not separate from titrations — it explains them.
An oxidant can only titrate a reductant if the cell E M F is positive, meaning its reduction potential is high enough to drive the reaction.

That is exactly why permanganate at plus one point five one volts and dichromate at plus one point three three are the workhorse titrants — they sit above common reductants like iron two plus at plus zero point seven seven, so their titrations run to completion.

The same data explains the hydrochloric-acid problem from a potential angle. The chlorine-chloride couple sits at plus one point three six volts — below permanganate, so permanganate is strong enough to oxidise chloride, but above the weaker dichromate, which is why dichromate can tolerate hydrochloric acid while permanganate cannot.
अब mirror procedure — galvanic cell predict या build करना।

Step one: दोनों half-reactions को reductions की तरह उनके standard potentials के साथ list करो। Step two: जिस half-cell का potential ज़्यादा है वो cathode बनता है, क्योंकि वो electrons को ज़्यादा ज़ोर से खींचता है, तो reduction वहाँ जीतता है; कम-potential वाला oxidation में forced होकर anode बनता है, उसका sign reverse होता है।

Step three: cell E M F cathode potential minus anode potential है, और positive value confirm करती है कि cell as written spontaneous है। Step four, और सबसे common slip: n balanced cell reaction में total electrons है, per atom नहीं।

Step five: energy और feasibility से जोड़ो। Standard Gibbs free energy change minus n times Faraday's constant times cell E M F है, और अगर equilibrium constant चाहिए, log K equals n times cell E M F over zero point zero five nine one।

यहाँ एक fast shortcut छुपा है — activity series। एक metal अपने से नीचे वाले metal के ion को displace करता है। Zinc, minus zero point seven six volts पे, copper को plus zero point three four पे displace करता है; पर zinc nitrate में copper spoon कुछ नहीं करता।
और यह रहा एक beautiful connection: <curious> electrode-potential idea titrations से अलग नहीं — यह उन्हें explain करता है।
एक oxidant किसी reductant को तभी titrate कर सकता है जब cell E M F positive हो, मतलब उसका reduction potential इतना ऊँचा हो कि reaction drive कर सके।

इसीलिए permanganate plus one point five one volts पे और dichromate plus one point three three पे workhorse titrants हैं — यह common reductants जैसे iron two plus को plus zero point seven seven पे ऊपर से देखते हैं, तो उनकी titrations completion तक चलती हैं।

यही data hydrochloric-acid problem को potential angle से explain करता है। Chlorine-chloride couple plus one point three six volts पे बैठा है — permanganate से नीचे, तो permanganate chloride को oxidise कर सकता है, पर कमज़ोर dichromate से ऊपर, इसीलिए dichromate hydrochloric acid tolerate कर लेता है जबकि permanganate नहीं।

board_events.text: Redox titration — the working equations

board_events.latex: n\text{-factor} = (\Delta\,\text{O.N. per atom}) \times (\text{number of such atoms})

board_events.text: \text{Endpoint: } \text{eq}_{ox} = \text{eq}_{red} \;\Rightarrow\; M_1 n_1 V_1 = M_2 n_2 V_2
n-factors (acidic): $MnO_4^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+}$ is $5$; $Cr_2O_7^{2-} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+}$ is $6$; $C_2O_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2CO_2$ is $2$; $Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}$ is $1$.
Medium changes $n$: $MnO_4^- \rightarrow MnO_2$ (neutral) is only $3$ electrons.
Units: equivalents, $n$ and $K$ are dimensionless; keep both volumes in the same unit.

segments.text: Now the working equations for titrations — few, and all built on one idea.
The n-factor of a species is the change in oxidation number per atom, times the number of such atoms — in short, the electrons it gains or loses per formula unit.
From it, equivalents equal moles times the n-factor, and normality equals molarity times the n-factor.
Milliequivalents are normality times volume in millilitres, which is the same as molarity times n times volume.
The endpoint condition is the heart of it: equivalents of oxidant equal equivalents of reductant, which becomes M one n one V one equals M two n two V two.

Keep these acidic n-factors at your fingertips: permanganate to manganese two plus is five; dichromate to two chromium three plus is six; oxalate to two carbon dioxide is two; and iron two plus to iron three plus is one.
But never forget the medium can change it: <whisper> permanganate going to manganese dioxide in neutral solution is only a three-electron oxidant, not five.
On units — equivalents, the n-factor, and the equilibrium constant are all dimensionless, and the one practical rule is to keep both volumes in the same unit.
अब titrations के working equations — कम हैं, और सब एक idea पे बने।
किसी species का n-factor है oxidation number change per atom, times ऐसे atoms की संख्या — short में, per formula unit जितने electrons वो gain या lose करती है।
इससे, equivalents equal moles times n-factor, और normality equals molarity times n-factor।
Milliequivalents normality times volume in millilitres हैं, जो वही है molarity times n times volume।
Endpoint condition दिल है: equivalents of oxidant equal equivalents of reductant, जो बन जाता है M one n one V one equals M two n two V two।
यह acidic n-factors उँगलियों पे रखो: permanganate to manganese two plus पाँच है; dichromate to two chromium three plus छह; oxalate to two carbon dioxide दो; और iron two plus to iron three plus एक।
पर कभी मत भूलो medium इसे बदल सकता है: <whisper> permanganate neutral solution में manganese dioxide जाकर सिर्फ three-electron oxidant है, पाँच नहीं।
Units पे — equivalents, n-factor, और equilibrium constant सब dimensionless हैं, और एक practical rule है दोनों volumes को एक ही unit में रखना।

sections.title: Electrochemical-cell formulas: EMF, free energy, equilibrium, Nernst

board_events.text: The four cell equations

board_events.latex: E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode} \quad (\text{both as reduction potentials})

board_events.text: Cell notation: anode $\mid$ anode soln $\parallel$ cathode soln $\mid$ cathode.
$n$ = electrons in the BALANCED cell reaction \u2014 for $Zn + 2Ag^+$, $n = 2$ even though the Ag half shows $1\,e^-$.
Units: $E$ in volts; $F$ in $\text{C mol}^{-1}$; $Q$ and $K$ dimensionless.

segments.text: Now the electrochemistry — four equations that do everything Class eleven asks.
First, the cell E M F is the cathode potential minus the anode potential, both taken as standard reduction potentials. A positive result means the cell runs as written.
The cell notation records this: anode on the left, then a phase line, the salt bridge as a double line, and the cathode on the right.

Second, the link to energy: the standard Gibbs free energy change equals minus n times Faraday's constant times the cell E M F, where Faraday's constant is ninety-six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole.
Third, the link to equilibrium: log K equals n times the cell E M F divided by zero point zero five nine one, at two hundred ninety-eight kelvin.
Fourth, the Nernst equation for non-standard conditions: the actual E M F equals the standard E M F minus zero point zero five nine one over n, times log of the reaction quotient Q.

One warning that trips up nearly everyone: <whisper> n is the number of electrons in the balanced cell reaction. For zinc plus two silver ions, n is two, even though the silver half-reaction is written with just one electron.
On units: the potential E is in volts, Faraday's constant is in coulombs per mole, and both the reaction quotient and the equilibrium constant are dimensionless.
अब electrochemistry — चार equations जो Class eleven की हर माँग पूरी करते हैं।
पहला, cell E M F cathode potential minus anode potential है, दोनों standard reduction potentials की तरह। Positive result मतलब cell as written चलता है।
Cell notation इसे record करता है: anode left पे, फिर phase line, salt bridge double line की तरह, और cathode right पे।
दूसरा, energy से link: standard Gibbs free energy change equals minus n times Faraday's constant times cell E M F, जहाँ Faraday's constant ninety-six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole है।
तीसरा, equilibrium से link: log K equals n times cell E M F over zero point zero five nine one, दो सौ अठानवे kelvin पे।
चौथा, non-standard conditions के लिए Nernst equation: actual E M F equals standard E M F minus zero point zero five nine one over n, times log of reaction quotient Q।
एक warning जो लगभग सबको गिराती है: <whisper> n balanced cell reaction में electrons की संख्या है। Zinc plus two silver ions के लिए, n दो है, भले ही silver half-reaction एक electron से लिखी हो।
Units पे: potential E volts में, Faraday's constant coulombs per mole में, और reaction quotient तथा equilibrium constant दोनों dimensionless।

sections.subtopic: Redox Titrations & Electrochemical Cells
sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): oxalic acid titrated against KMnO4

board_events.text: Find the volume of $KMnO_4$ needed
20.0 mL of 0.10 M oxalic acid vs 0.020 M $KMnO_4$ in dilute $H_2SO_4$.
n-factors: oxalate $C_2O_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2CO_2$ gives $n = 2$; permanganate $MnO_4^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+}$ gives $n = 5$.
Endpoint: $M_{KMnO_4}\,n\,V = M_{oxalic}\,n\,V$
Self-indicating: the first excess drop turns the flask permanent pink.
Answer: 40.0 mL of $KMnO_4$.

segments.text: A clean C B S E titration: twenty point zero millilitres of zero point one zero molar oxalic acid is titrated against zero point zero two zero molar permanganate in dilute sulphuric acid. Find the volume of permanganate needed.
Read off the four numbers first, then get the n-factors, because everything hinges on them.
Oxalate going to two carbon dioxide is a two-electron reductant, so its n-factor is two. Permanganate going to manganese two plus in acid is a five-electron oxidant, so its n-factor is five.
Now write the endpoint balance: molarity times n-factor times volume for the permanganate equals the same product for the oxalic acid.
Substitute: zero point zero two zero times five times V equals zero point one zero times two times twenty point zero.
That simplifies to zero point one zero V equals four point zero, so V is forty point zero millilitres.
And you know you have hit it exactly, because permanganate is self-indicating — the first excess drop turns the flask permanent pink.
So the answer is forty point zero millilitres of permanganate.

एक clean C B S E titration: twenty point zero millilitres of zero point one zero molar oxalic acid को zero point zero two zero molar permanganate के against dilute sulphuric acid में titrate किया जाता है। Permanganate का needed volume निकालो।
पहले चारों numbers पढ़ो, फिर n-factors निकालो, क्योंकि सब कुछ उन्हीं पे टिका है।
Oxalate two carbon dioxide जाकर two-electron reductant है, तो n-factor दो। Permanganate acid में manganese two plus जाकर five-electron oxidant है, तो n-factor पाँच।
अब endpoint balance लिखो: permanganate के लिए molarity times n-factor times volume equal oxalic acid के लिए वही product।
Substitute करो: zero point zero two zero times five times V equals zero point one zero times two times twenty point zero।
यह simplify होता है zero point one zero V equals four point zero, तो V forty point zero millilitres।
और तुम्हें exactly पता चलता है कि पहुँच गए, क्योंकि permanganate self-indicating है — पहला excess drop flask को permanent pink कर देता है।
तो answer forty point zero millilitres permanganate।

sections.subtopic: Redox Titrations & Electrochemical Cells
sections.title: Worked example (NEET speed trap): strongest reductant & largest EMF

board_events.text: Read strengths straight off the $E^\circ$ values
Most positive $E^\circ$ → strongest oxidising agent (the ion) → here $Ag^+$.
Most negative $E^\circ$ → its metal is the strongest reducing agent → here $Zn$.
Largest EMF → the pair with the widest $E^\circ$ gap.
Trap: equating 'most positive $E^\circ$' with 'best reducing agent' — it is exactly the opposite.
Answer: (i) $Zn$ is the strongest reducing agent; (ii) the $Zn$-$Ag$ cell gives the largest EMF.

segments.text: This N E E T trap rewards reading strengths straight off the potentials, with no lengthy calculation.
You are given three standard potentials: silver at plus zero point eight zero volts, copper at plus zero point three four, and zinc at minus zero point seven six.
The first mental rule: the most positive potential marks the strongest oxidising agent — here that is the silver ion, which loves electrons most.
The second rule is the mirror: the most negative potential means its metal is the strongest reducing agent. So zinc metal is the best reducer here.
For the largest E M F, you want the pair with the widest gap in potential.
That is zinc with silver: zero point eight zero minus negative zero point seven six is one point five six volts, comfortably beating the zinc-copper pair at one point one zero.

Beware the classic trap: <curious> equating most positive potential with best reducing agent. It is exactly backwards — a high reduction potential means the species loves electrons, making it a strong oxidant and a poor reducer.
So the answer: zinc is the strongest reducing agent, and the zinc-silver cell gives the largest E M F.
यह N E E T trap strengths को सीधे potentials से पढ़ने पे reward देता है, बिना lengthy calculation।
तुम्हें तीन standard potentials दिए हैं: silver plus zero point eight zero volts पे, copper plus zero point three four पे, और zinc minus zero point seven six पे।
पहला mental rule: सबसे positive potential strongest oxidising agent बताता है — यहाँ वो silver ion है, जो electrons सबसे ज़्यादा चाहता है।
दूसरा rule mirror है: सबसे negative potential मतलब उसका metal strongest reducing agent। तो zinc metal यहाँ सबसे अच्छा reducer है।
सबसे बड़े E M F के लिए, तुम्हें वो pair चाहिए जिसका potential gap सबसे widest हो।
वो zinc with silver है: zero point eight zero minus negative zero point seven six is one point five six volts, comfortably zinc-copper pair one point one zero को beat करते हुए।

उस classic trap से बचो: <curious> most positive potential को best reducing agent समझना। यह ठीक उल्टा है — high reduction potential मतलब species electrons से प्यार करती है, अच्छा oxidant और poor reducer।
तो answer: zinc strongest reducing agent है, और zinc-silver cell सबसे बड़ा E M F देता है।

segments.text: Now a J E E Main problem linking electrode potential to thermodynamics — the classic zinc-silver cell.
The cell is zinc against its ion, salt bridge, silver ion against silver, all at one molar. Silver's potential is plus zero point eight zero volts, zinc's is minus zero point seven six.
First write the balanced cell reaction: silver is reduced and zinc oxidised, so zinc plus two silver ions gives zinc two plus plus two silver.
The cell E M F is the cathode minus the anode: plus zero point eight zero minus negative zero point seven six, which is one point five six volts.
Now the step that catches people: <excited> n is two, not one. The balanced reaction reduces two silver ions, even though the silver half-reaction is written with a single electron.

The diagram shows the whole cell: zinc as the anode losing electrons, silver as the cathode gaining them, the salt bridge keeping both sides neutral, and the voltmeter reading one point five six volts.

Now the free energy: the standard Gibbs free energy change is minus n times Faraday's constant times the cell E M F, which is minus two times ninety-six thousand five hundred times one point five six.
That works out to minus three point zero one times ten to the fifth joules, or about minus three hundred one kilojoules.

The negative sign confirms the reaction is spontaneous. So the answer: the cell E M F is one point five six volts, and the standard Gibbs free energy change is about minus three hundred one kilojoules.
अब एक J E E Main problem जो electrode potential को thermodynamics से जोड़ता है — classic zinc-silver cell।
Cell है zinc अपने ion के against, salt bridge, silver ion silver के against, सब one molar पे। Silver का potential plus zero point eight zero volts, zinc का minus zero point seven six।
पहले balanced cell reaction लिखो: silver reduce होता है और zinc oxidise, तो zinc plus two silver ions देता है zinc two plus plus two silver।
Cell E M F cathode minus anode है: plus zero point eight zero minus negative zero point seven six, जो one point five six volts।
अब वो step जो लोगों को पकड़ता है: <excited> n दो है, एक नहीं। Balanced reaction दो silver ions reduce करती है, भले ही silver half-reaction एक single electron से लिखी हो।
Diagram पूरा cell दिखाता है: zinc anode की तरह electrons खोता, silver cathode की तरह उन्हें पाता, salt bridge दोनों sides को neutral रखता, और voltmeter one point five six volts पढ़ता।
अब free energy: standard Gibbs free energy change minus n times Faraday's constant times cell E M F है, जो minus two times ninety-six thousand five hundred times one point five six।
यह minus three point zero one times ten to the fifth joules आता है, या लगभग minus three hundred one kilojoules।
Negative sign confirm करता है कि reaction spontaneous है। तो answer: cell E M F one point five six volts, और standard Gibbs free energy change लगभग minus three hundred one kilojoules।

sections.subtopic: Redox Titrations & Electrochemical Cells
sections.title: Worked example (JEE Advanced): does Cu+ disproportionate?

board_events.text: Use $E^\circ$ to test $Cu^+$ stability
$Cu^+ + e^- \rightarrow Cu$, $E^\circ = +0.52$ V; $\quad Cu^{2+} + e^- \rightarrow Cu^+$, $E^\circ = +0.16$ V.
Set up $2Cu^+ \rightarrow Cu + Cu^{2+}$ as a cell: one $Cu^+$ reduced (cathode), one oxidised (anode).
Cathode: $Cu^+/Cu$ at $+0.52$; anode: $Cu^{2+}/Cu^+$ at $+0.16$.
$E^\circ_{cell} \gt 0 \Rightarrow$ spontaneous \u2014 $Cu^+$ is unstable in water.
The large $K$ is why cuprous salts are rare in water while $Cu^{2+}$ dominates.

segments.text: The J E E Advanced problem chains disproportionation to electrode potentials — will the cuprous ion, copper one plus, survive in water?
You are given two couples: copper one plus to copper metal at plus zero point five two volts, and copper two plus to copper one plus at plus zero point one six.

Set up the disproportionation, two copper one plus giving copper plus copper two plus, as a little cell: one copper one plus is reduced to the metal at the cathode, the other is oxidised to copper two plus at the anode.
So the cathode is the copper-one-plus-to-copper couple at plus zero point five two, and the anode is the copper-two-plus-to-copper-one-plus couple at plus zero point one six.
The cell E M F is zero point five two minus zero point one six, which is plus zero point three six volts.
Since the cell E M F is positive, the disproportionation is spontaneous — copper one plus is unstable in water.

Now the equilibrium constant. Here only one electron is transferred overall, so log K is one times zero point three six over zero point zero five nine one, about six point zero nine, giving K around one point two times ten to the sixth.
That huge K is the real-world punchline: <chuckle> it is exactly why cuprous salts are rare in water while copper two plus dominates.
J E E Advanced problem disproportionation को electrode potentials से chain करता है — क्या cuprous ion, copper one plus, water में survive करेगा?
तुम्हें दो couples दिए हैं: copper one plus to copper metal plus zero point five two volts पे, और copper two plus to copper one plus plus zero point one six पे।

Disproportionation, two copper one plus देता है copper plus copper two plus, को एक छोटे cell की तरह set up करो: एक copper one plus cathode पे metal में reduce होता, दूसरा anode पे copper two plus में oxidise।
तो cathode copper-one-plus-to-copper couple plus zero point five two पे, और anode copper-two-plus-to-copper-one-plus couple plus zero point one six पे।
Cell E M F zero point five two minus zero point one six है, जो plus zero point three six volts।
चूँकि cell E M F positive है, disproportionation spontaneous है — copper one plus water में unstable है।

अब equilibrium constant। यहाँ overall सिर्फ एक electron transfer होता है, तो log K one times zero point three six over zero point zero five nine one है, लगभग six point zero nine, देता हुआ K around one point two times ten to the sixth।
वो huge K real-world punchline है: <chuckle> यही वजह है कि cuprous salts water में rare हैं जबकि copper two plus dominate करता है।

sections.subtopic: Redox Titrations & Electrochemical Cells
sections.title: Pitfalls & pro-tips: equivalents, n-counting, and reading $E^\circ$

board_events.text: The four traps
Equating moles instead of equivalents — at the endpoint it is equivalents (moles $\times$ n-factor) that match, never raw moles.
Using the wrong n-factor for the medium \u2014 $MnO_4^-$ is a 5-electron oxidant in acid but only 3 in neutral/mild base.
Mis-counting $n$ in cell EMF \u2014 $n$ is the electrons in the balanced reaction; for $Zn + 2Ag^+$, $n = 2$.
Sign errors and the wrong electron path \u2014 always $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$; electrons travel through the wire, anode $\\rightarrow$ cathode.
Pro-tip
Titrations: write everything as $M\,n\,V$ on each side and equate \u2014 the unknown pops out in one line, no balanced equation needed.
Cells: rank the $E^\circ$ values first — higher = cathode, lower = anode, EMF is the gap. A negative gap means you drew the cell backwards; swap the electrodes.

segments.text: Let's close titrations and cells with the four traps that cost marks, then two habits that beat them.

First, and most common: equating moles instead of equivalents. At the endpoint it is equivalents — moles times the n-factor — that match, never raw moles. Forgetting the n-factor is the classic titration error.
Second: using the wrong n-factor for the medium. Permanganate is a five-electron oxidant in acid, but only a three-electron oxidant in neutral or mildly basic solution. Decide the medium first.
Third: mis-counting n in the cell E M F. n is the electrons in the balanced cell reaction — for zinc plus two silver ions, n is two, even though the silver half shows one electron.

Fourth: sign errors and the wrong electron path. It is always cathode minus anode, both as reduction potentials, and electrons travel through the wire from anode to cathode, never through the salt bridge.
Now the pro-tips. For titrations, write everything as molarity times n times volume on each side and equate them.
The unknown pops out in a single line — you never need to balance the full equation.

For cells, rank the standard potentials first: <whisper> higher is the cathode, lower is the anode, and the E M F is just the gap. A negative gap means you have drawn the cell backwards, so swap the electrodes rather than redoing the algebra.
Titrations और cells को उन चार traps के साथ बंद करते हैं जो marks खाते हैं, फिर दो habits जो उन्हें beat करती हैं।
पहला, और सबसे common: moles के बदले equivalents equate करना। Endpoint पे equivalents — moles times n-factor — match करते हैं, कभी raw moles नहीं। n-factor भूलना classic titration error है।
दूसरा: medium के लिए गलत n-factor use करना। Permanganate acid में five-electron oxidant है, पर neutral या mildly basic में सिर्फ three-electron। Medium पहले decide करो।
तीसरा: cell E M F में n mis-count करना। n balanced cell reaction में electrons है — zinc plus two silver ions के लिए, n दो है, भले ही silver half एक electron दिखाए।
चौथा: sign errors और गलत electron path। हमेशा cathode minus anode, दोनों reduction potentials की तरह, और electrons wire से anode से cathode जाते हैं, salt bridge से कभी नहीं।
अब pro-tips। Titrations के लिए, हर side पे molarity times n times volume लिखो और equate करो।
Unknown एक single line में निकल आता है — तुम्हें कभी full equation balance करने की ज़रूरत नहीं।

Cells के लिए, पहले standard potentials rank करो: <whisper> ऊँचा cathode है, नीचा anode, और E M F बस gap है। Negative gap मतलब तुमने cell उल्टा बनाया, तो algebra दोबारा करने के बजाय electrodes swap कर दो।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: The four families of redox reactions

board_events.text: Almost every redox reaction is one of four shapes
Combination: two things join into one, with an O.N. change — $2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO$.
Decomposition: one thing splits into two or more, with an O.N. change — $2KClO_3 \rightarrow 2KCl + 3O_2$.
Displacement: one species kicks out another and takes its place — $Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu$.
Disproportionation: a single element at one middling O.N. splits — some atoms climb, others fall.
Learning to spot the family on sight turns a scary equation into a two-second classification.
Like cricket shots — cover drive, pull, sweep, cut — once you know the four strokes, every shot is a variation.
So too here: master four families and every redox equation becomes recognisable.

segments.text: You now know how electrons move in a redox reaction. This subtopic is about recognising the shapes these reactions come in — because almost every one you will ever meet falls into just four families.
The first is combination: two things join into one, and in doing so electrons shift. Magnesium meets oxygen and they fuse into magnesium oxide.
The second is decomposition, the reverse stroke: one thing splits into two or more, with electrons redistributing. Heated potassium chlorate breaks into potassium chloride and oxygen.

The third is displacement: one species kicks out another and takes its place, because it wants the electrons more. Drop a zinc strip into blue copper sulphate and the zinc shoves copper out of solution, the blue fading away.

The fourth is the strangest and most beautiful: disproportionation. A single element, sitting at one middling oxidation state, splits its own fate — some atoms climb to a higher state while others fall to a lower one, in the very same reaction.
Here is the payoff: <curious> learning to spot the family on sight turns a scary-looking equation into a two-second classification.
Think of recognising cricket shots. A cover drive, a pull, a sweep, a cut — once you know the four basic strokes, every shot a batsman plays is just a variation.
Redox reactions are exactly the same. Master these four families, and every redox equation you meet becomes instantly recognisable.

तुम्हें अब पता है redox reaction में electrons कैसे move करते हैं। यह subtopic उन shapes को पहचानने के बारे में है जिनमें यह reactions आती हैं — क्योंकि लगभग हर एक जो तुम मिलोगे सिर्फ चार families में आती है।
पहली combination है: दो चीज़ें एक में जुड़ती हैं, और ऐसा करते हुए electrons shift होते हैं। Magnesium oxygen से मिलता है और वो magnesium oxide में fuse हो जाते हैं।
दूसरी decomposition है, reverse stroke: एक चीज़ दो या ज़्यादा में split होती है, electrons redistribute करते हुए। गरम potassium chlorate potassium chloride और oxygen में टूटता है।

तीसरी displacement है: एक species दूसरी को निकालकर उसकी जगह लेती है, क्योंकि वो electrons ज़्यादा चाहती है। Zinc strip को नीले copper sulphate में डालो और zinc copper को solution से बाहर धकेल देता है, नीला fade होता हुआ।

चौथी सबसे अजीब और सबसे beautiful है: disproportionation। एक single element, एक middling oxidation state पे बैठा, अपनी fate split करता है — कुछ atoms higher state पे चढ़ते हैं जबकि कुछ lower पे गिरते हैं, उसी reaction में।
यह रहा payoff: <curious> family को देखते ही पहचानना एक scary-looking equation को two-second classification बना देता है।
Cricket shots पहचानना सोचो। Cover drive, pull, sweep, cut — एक बार चार basic strokes आ जाएँ, batsman का हर shot बस एक variation है।
Redox reactions बिल्कुल वैसे ही हैं। इन चार families को master करो, और हर redox equation instantly recognisable हो जाती है।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: Competitive electron transfer, the reactivity series, and two cautions

board_events.text: The tug-of-war for electrons
Place zinc in copper sulphate and you are really asking: who wants these electrons more, zinc or copper? Copper wins, so copper deposits and zinc dissolves.
Rank every metal by how easily it gives up electrons and you get the reactivity (activity) series — the master league-table for such contests.
The same competition runs for non-metals: a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one ($Cl_2$ frees $Br_2$ from a bromide).
Caution 1: not every combination or decomposition is redox — $CaO + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3$ has no O.N. change, so it is NOT redox.
Caution 2: disproportionation needs an element in an intermediate O.N. (a higher and a lower state both available).
So always assign O.N. and check for a change before you classify.
An element already at its maximum (Mn in $MnO_4^-$) or minimum cannot disproportionate.

segments.text: Underneath every displacement reaction is one deep idea: competitive electron transfer, a tug-of-war for electrons.

When you place zinc in copper sulphate, you are really asking a question: who wants these electrons more, zinc or copper? Copper wins, so copper ions grab zinc's electrons and deposit as metal, while the zinc dissolves.

Rank every metal by how badly it wants to keep its electrons — that is, how easily it gives them up — and you get the reactivity, or activity, series: the master league-table that predicts the winner of any such contest before you even mix the chemicals.

The same competition runs in reverse for non-metals. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one — chlorine frees bromine from a bromide — because chlorine's pull on electrons beats bromine's.

Now two cautions examiners love. First: <whisper> not every combination or decomposition is a redox reaction. Calcium oxide plus carbon dioxide gives calcium carbonate, a combination — but no oxidation number changes, so it is not redox.
Second: disproportionation needs an element in an intermediate oxidation state, one with both a higher and a lower state available.
So the safe habit is always to assign oxidation numbers and check for a change before you classify anything.
And an element already at its maximum — like manganese in permanganate — or at its minimum simply cannot disproportionate, because there is nowhere left to climb or fall.
हर displacement reaction के नीचे एक deep idea है: competitive electron transfer, electrons के लिए tug-of-war।

जब तुम zinc को copper sulphate में डालते हो, तुम असल में एक सवाल पूछ रहे हो: कौन electrons ज़्यादा चाहता है, zinc या copper? Copper जीतता है, तो copper ions zinc के electrons पकड़कर metal की तरह deposit होते हैं, जबकि zinc dissolve हो जाता है।

हर metal को rank करो कि वो electrons कितनी आसानी से देता है — और तुम्हें reactivity, या activity, series मिलती है: master league-table जो ऐसे किसी भी contest का winner chemicals mix करने से पहले predict कर देती है।

यही competition non-metals के लिए reverse चलती है। एक ज़्यादा reactive halogen कम reactive को displace करता है — chlorine bromide से bromine free करता है — क्योंकि chlorine का electrons पे pull bromine से beat करता है।

अब दो cautions जो examiners को पसंद हैं। पहला: <whisper> हर combination या decomposition redox reaction नहीं है। Calcium oxide plus carbon dioxide देता है calcium carbonate, एक combination — पर कोई oxidation number change नहीं, तो यह redox नहीं।
दूसरा: disproportionation को एक intermediate oxidation state वाला element चाहिए, जिसके पास higher और lower दोनों state available हों।
तो safe habit है हमेशा oxidation numbers assign करना और change check करना, कुछ भी classify करने से पहले।
और एक element जो already अपने maximum पे है — जैसे permanganate में manganese — या minimum पे, disproportionate कर ही नहीं सकता, क्योंकि चढ़ने या गिरने को कुछ बचा ही नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: Formal definitions: the four types, comproportionation & intramolecular redox

board_events.text: The four types, defined
Combination redox: $A + B \rightarrow AB$ with at least one O.N. change (e.g. $C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2$).
Decomposition redox: $AB \rightarrow A + B$ with O.N. changes — the reverse of combination (e.g. electrolysis of water).
Displacement redox: $A + BC \rightarrow AC + B$; sub-types are metal, hydrogen, and halogen displacement.
Disproportionation: one element in a single intermediate O.N. is simultaneously oxidised AND reduced (e.g. $2H_2O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O + O_2$).
Comproportionation: the reverse — two different O.N. states of one element converge to a single state ($2H_2S + SO_2 \rightarrow 3S + 2H_2O$).
Intramolecular redox: two DIFFERENT elements change oppositely inside one compound — distinct from disproportionation.
Classification itself is qualitative — it carries no units.

segments.text: Let's pin down the four types formally, so you can quote them cleanly.
A combination redox is A plus B giving A B, with at least one element changing oxidation number — for instance carbon plus oxygen giving carbon dioxide.
A decomposition redox is the reverse: A B splitting into A plus B, with oxidation-number changes, as when water is electrolysed into hydrogen and oxygen.
A displacement redox is A plus B C giving A C plus B, where A displaces B. Its sub-types are metal displacement, hydrogen displacement, and halogen displacement.

Disproportionation is the special one: a single element in one intermediate oxidation state is oxidised and reduced at the same time — hydrogen peroxide breaking into water and oxygen is the classic case.

Its mirror image is comproportionation: <curious> two different oxidation states of the same element converge to a single intermediate state, as when hydrogen sulphide and sulphur dioxide react to give sulphur and water.

And a rarer cousin: intramolecular redox, where two different elements change in opposite directions inside one compound. That is distinct from disproportionation, which needs a single element splitting.
Finally, note that classification itself is purely qualitative — it is a label, carrying no units.
चार types को formally pin down करते हैं, ताकि तुम इन्हें cleanly quote कर सको।
Combination redox है A plus B देता है A B, कम से कम एक element का oxidation number बदलते हुए — जैसे carbon plus oxygen देता है carbon dioxide।
Decomposition redox reverse है: A B split होकर A plus B, oxidation-number changes के साथ, जैसे water electrolyse होकर hydrogen और oxygen में।
Displacement redox है A plus B C देता है A C plus B, जहाँ A, B को displace करता है। इसके sub-types हैं metal displacement, hydrogen displacement, और halogen displacement।
Disproportionation special है: एक single element एक intermediate oxidation state पे एक साथ oxidise और reduce होता है — hydrogen peroxide का water और oxygen में टूटना classic case है।

इसका mirror image है comproportionation: <curious> एक ही element के दो अलग oxidation states एक single intermediate state पे converge करते हैं, जैसे hydrogen sulphide और sulphur dioxide react करके sulphur और water देते हैं।
और एक rarer cousin: intramolecular redox, जहाँ दो अलग elements एक compound के अंदर opposite directions में बदलते हैं। यह disproportionation से distinct है, जिसे single element splitting चाहिए।
आखिर में, note करो कि classification खुद purely qualitative है — यह एक label है, बिना किसी unit के।

board_events.text: Order (high → low): $K \gt Na \gt Ca \gt Mg \gt Al \gt Zn \gt Fe \gt Pb \gt (H) \gt Cu \gt Hg \gt Ag \gt Au$.
A metal higher in the series displaces the ion of any metal lower than it; metals above (H) liberate $H_2$ from acids.
Halogen reactivity (displacing power): $F_2 \gt Cl_2 \gt Br_2 \gt I_2$.
Stock notation
Write the O.N. as a Roman numeral in parentheses, no space, no sign for positive values — iron(III), copper(II), manganese(VII).
$Fe_3O_4$ is a mixed oxide, $FeO \cdot Fe_2O_3$ — one Fe(II) and two Fe(III); Stock notation honestly records both.

segments.text: The reactivity series is the league-table you will reach for constantly, so let's read it carefully.
The ladder on the board runs from the most reactive metal at the top to the least reactive at the bottom.
In order, from high to low: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, then hydrogen in brackets, then copper, mercury, silver, and gold.
The rule it encodes: a metal higher in the series displaces the ion of any metal lower than it, and any metal above hydrogen liberates hydrogen gas from acids.
For non-metals there is a parallel order — halogen displacing power runs fluorine, then chlorine, then bromine, then iodine, most reactive to least.
Now Stock notation, a small but examiner-favourite skill.
You write the oxidation number as a Roman numeral in parentheses, with no space and no sign for positive values — so iron three, copper two, manganese seven.

And a subtle case worth remembering: <curious> iron three oxide, Fe three O four, is actually a mixed oxide of iron two oxide and iron three oxide — one iron two and two iron three — and Stock notation honestly records both real states rather than a misleading average.
Reactivity series वो league-table है जिसे तुम बार बार reach करोगे, तो इसे carefully पढ़ते हैं।
Board पे ladder सबसे reactive metal से ऊपर से सबसे कम reactive तक नीचे चलता है।
Order में, high से low: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, फिर hydrogen brackets में, फिर copper, mercury, silver, और gold।
यह जो rule encode करता है: series में ऊँचा metal अपने से नीचे किसी metal के ion को displace करता है, और hydrogen से ऊपर कोई भी metal acids से hydrogen gas liberate करता है।
Non-metals के लिए एक parallel order है — halogen displacing power चलता है fluorine, फिर chlorine, फिर bromine, फिर iodine, सबसे reactive से कम।
अब Stock notation, एक छोटी पर examiner-favourite skill।
तुम oxidation number को parentheses में Roman numeral की तरह लिखते हो, बिना space और positive values के लिए बिना sign — तो iron three, copper two, manganese seven।

और एक subtle case याद रखने लायक: <curious> iron three oxide, Fe three O four, असल में iron two oxide और iron three oxide का mixed oxide है — एक iron two और दो iron three — और Stock notation misleading average के बजाय दोनों real states honestly record करता है।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: How to classify, predict displacement, and the honest limits of O.N.

board_events.text: Classify a redox reaction — step by step
Step 1: assign O.N. to every element on both sides. Step 2: confirm it is redox at all — if no O.N. changes, it is not redox.
Step 3: count how many substances combine or split and how many elements change state, then read off the family.
Predict a displacement
Locate both species in the series; the higher (more reactive) one displaces the lower. If the added species is lower, no reaction occurs — a copper rod in $ZnSO_4$ does nothing.
The honest limits of the O.N. idea
O.N. is a hypothetical charge from an arbitrary convention — not the real charge; fractional/average values (like $+2.5$ in $S_4O_6^{2-}$) describe no single atom.
For many organic and chain compounds, like-atom bonds (C–C, O–O) make O.N. assignment ambiguous.
O.N. is NOT valency — valency is an unsigned bonding capacity; O.N. carries a sign and can differ in magnitude.

segments.text: Here is the procedure for classifying any redox reaction, followed by two things every master student should keep honest about.

Step one: assign oxidation numbers to every element on both sides. Step two: confirm it is redox at all — if no oxidation number changes, it is not a redox reaction, and that single check kills the most common trap.

Step three: count how many substances combine or split, and how many elements change state, then read off the family — two into one is combination, one into many is decomposition, a free element ousting a combined one is displacement, and one element ending in both a higher and a lower state is disproportionation.
To predict a displacement, use the series.

Locate both species in it; the higher, more reactive one displaces the lower. If the species you add sits lower than the one in the compound, nothing happens — a copper rod in zinc sulphate just sits there.
Now the honest limits, because oxidation number is a model, not reality.

It is a hypothetical charge from an arbitrary electron-sharing convention, not the real charge on an atom — and a fractional or average value, like plus two point five in tetrathionate, describes no single atom at all.
For many organic and chain compounds, like-atom bonds — carbon to carbon, oxygen to oxygen — make the assignment genuinely ambiguous.
And keep this straight: <whisper> oxidation number is not valency. Valency is an unsigned bonding capacity; oxidation number carries a sign and can differ in magnitude.
यह रहा किसी भी redox reaction को classify करने का procedure, उसके बाद दो चीज़ें जिनके बारे में हर master student को honest रहना चाहिए।

Step one: दोनों side के हर element को oxidation numbers assign करो। Step two: confirm करो कि यह redox है भी या नहीं — अगर कोई oxidation number नहीं बदलता, यह redox reaction नहीं, और यह एक check सबसे common trap को मार देता है।

Step three: गिनो कितनी substances combine या split होती हैं, और कितने elements state बदलते हैं, फिर family पढ़ो — दो का एक combination, एक का कई decomposition, एक free element एक combined को निकालना displacement, और एक element का higher और lower दोनों state पे खत्म होना disproportionation।
Displacement predict करने को, series use करो।

दोनों species को इसमें locate करो; ऊँचा, ज़्यादा reactive वाला नीचे को displace करता है। अगर जो species तुम add करते हो वो compound वाले से नीचे बैठे, कुछ नहीं होता — zinc sulphate में copper rod बस बैठा रहता है।
अब honest limits, क्योंकि oxidation number एक model है, reality नहीं।

यह एक arbitrary electron-sharing convention से hypothetical charge है, atom का real charge नहीं — और fractional या average value, जैसे tetrathionate में plus two point five, किसी single atom को describe करता ही नहीं।
कई organic और chain compounds के लिए, like-atom bonds — carbon to carbon, oxygen to oxygen — assignment को genuinely ambiguous बना देते हैं।
और यह straight रखो: <whisper> oxidation number valency नहीं है। Valency एक unsigned bonding capacity है; oxidation number sign के साथ आता है और magnitude में अलग हो सकता है।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: Redox in action: where it runs the world

board_events.text: Redox is not abstract — it runs the world
Corrosion (rusting): iron is oxidised by $O_2$ and moisture; prevented by galvanisation (sacrificial zinc) and cathodic protection.
Combustion & respiration: burning fuels and cellular respiration both oxidise carbon compounds with $O_2$, releasing energy.
Electrochemical cells: dry cells, lead-storage batteries, and fuel cells are controlled redox packaged to deliver electricity.
Metallurgy: most metals are extracted by reduction of their ores — iron oxide by $CO$, reactive metals like $Al$ by electrolysis.
Bleaching & disinfection: $Cl_2$ and $H_2O_2$ bleach by oxidising coloured compounds; $KMnO_4$ and $H_2O_2$ act as antiseptics.
Photography & electroplating: film relies on reduction of $Ag^+$ to silver; electroplating deposits metal by cathodic reduction.
Recognising the redox skeleton inside each turns 'facts to memorise' into one idea applied many ways.

segments.text: This is not abstract theory — redox runs the world around you, and seeing it everywhere is what makes the chapter stick.

Start with corrosion. Rusting is iron being oxidised by atmospheric oxygen and moisture. We fight it with galvanisation — a sacrificial zinc coat that, being more reactive, oxidises instead of the iron — and with cathodic protection.

Combustion and respiration are the same chemistry at different scales: burning fuels and cellular respiration both oxidise carbon compounds with oxygen, releasing energy — the reaction powering an engine and a living cell alike.
Electrochemical cells are controlled redox packaged to deliver electricity: dry cells, lead-storage batteries, and fuel cells.
Metallurgy leans on it too — most metals are extracted by reducing their ores, iron oxide by carbon monoxide in the blast furnace, and reactive metals like aluminium by electrolytic reduction.

Bleaching and disinfection are oxidations: chlorine and hydrogen peroxide bleach by oxidising coloured compounds, and permanganate and hydrogen peroxide act as antiseptics by oxidising microbial matter.
Even photography and electroplating: film relies on the reduction of silver ions to metallic silver, and electroplating deposits a metal by cathodic reduction.
The real lesson is unification: <curious> recognising the redox skeleton inside each of these turns a pile of facts to memorise into one idea applied many different ways.
यह abstract theory नहीं — redox तुम्हारे आस-पास की दुनिया चलाता है, और इसे हर जगह देखना ही chapter को stick कराता है।

Corrosion से शुरू। Rusting iron का atmospheric oxygen और moisture से oxidise होना है। हम इससे galvanisation से लड़ते हैं — एक sacrificial zinc coat जो, ज़्यादा reactive होने से, iron के बजाय खुद oxidise होता है — और cathodic protection से।

Combustion और respiration अलग scales पे वही chemistry हैं: fuels जलाना और cellular respiration दोनों carbon compounds को oxygen से oxidise करते हैं, energy release करते हुए — वही reaction जो engine और living cell दोनों को power देती है।
Electrochemical cells controlled redox हैं जो electricity deliver करने के लिए packaged हैं: dry cells, lead-storage batteries, और fuel cells।
Metallurgy भी इस पर टिकी है — ज़्यादातर metals अपने ores को reduce करके निकाले जाते हैं, iron oxide blast furnace में carbon monoxide से, और reactive metals जैसे aluminium electrolytic reduction से।

Bleaching और disinfection oxidations हैं: chlorine और hydrogen peroxide coloured compounds को oxidise करके bleach करते हैं, और permanganate तथा hydrogen peroxide microbial matter को oxidise करके antiseptics की तरह act करते हैं।
यहाँ तक कि photography और electroplating: film silver ions के metallic silver में reduction पे टिकी है, और electroplating cathodic reduction से metal deposit करता है।
असली lesson unification है: <curious> इन सब के अंदर redox skeleton पहचानना ratne वाले facts के ढेर को एक idea बना देता है जो कई अलग तरीकों से apply होता है।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): classify three reactions

board_events.text: Classify each; state whether it is redox
(i) Cl: $+5 \rightarrow -1$ (reduced); O: $-2 \rightarrow 0$ (oxidised). One reactant → two products with O.N. change → decomposition redox.
(ii) Ca stays $+2$, C stays $+4$, O stays $-2$ — no O.N. change → combination, but NOT redox.
(iii) Fe: $0 \rightarrow +2$ (oxidised); Cu: $+2 \rightarrow 0$ (reduced); a free metal displaces a combined one → metal-displacement redox.
Answer: (i) decomposition (redox); (ii) combination (non-redox); (iii) displacement (redox).

segments.text: A C B S E staple: classify each reaction and state whether it is redox. The discipline is to assign oxidation numbers first, every time.
The first reaction is potassium chlorate decomposing on heating into potassium chloride and oxygen.

Track the numbers: chlorine falls from plus five to minus one, so it is reduced, while oxygen rises from minus two to zero, so it is oxidised. One reactant splitting into two products with an oxidation-number change makes this a decomposition redox.
The second is calcium oxide plus carbon dioxide giving calcium carbonate.
Check every element: calcium stays plus two, carbon stays plus four, oxygen stays minus two. Nothing changes, so although this is a combination, it is not a redox reaction — the classic trap.
The third is iron plus copper sulphate giving iron sulphate plus copper.
Iron goes from zero to plus two, oxidised; copper goes from plus two to zero, reduced. A free metal displacing a combined one makes this a metal-displacement redox.
So the answer set: decomposition and redox; combination but not redox; and displacement and redox.
एक C B S E staple: हर reaction classify करो और बताओ redox है या नहीं। Discipline है हर बार पहले oxidation numbers assign करना।
पहली reaction है potassium chlorate गरम होने पे potassium chloride और oxygen में decompose होता।

Numbers track करो: chlorine plus five से minus one गिरता है, तो reduced, जबकि oxygen minus two से zero चढ़ता है, तो oxidised। एक reactant का दो products में split होना oxidation-number change के साथ इसे decomposition redox बनाता है।
दूसरी है calcium oxide plus carbon dioxide देता है calcium carbonate।
हर element check करो: calcium plus two रहता है, carbon plus four, oxygen minus two। कुछ नहीं बदलता, तो यह combination होते हुए भी redox reaction नहीं — classic trap।
तीसरी है iron plus copper sulphate देता है iron sulphate plus copper।
Iron zero से plus two जाता है, oxidised; copper plus two से zero, reduced। एक free metal का combined को displace करना इसे metal-displacement redox बनाता है।
तो answer set: decomposition और redox; combination पर redox नहीं; और displacement और redox।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: Worked example (NEET speed trap): which pair reacts?

board_events.text: A metal reacts only if it sits ABOVE the salt's metal
Options: (a) $Cu + ZnSO_4$; (b) $Ag + CuSO_4$; (c) $Zn + FeSO_4$; (d) $Cu + Al_2(SO_4)_3$.
Mental rule: check the direction in the activity series before predicting.
(a) Cu is below Zn — no reaction.
(b) Ag is below Cu — no reaction.
(c) Zn is above Fe \u2014 reacts! $Zn + FeSO_4 \\rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Fe$.
(d) Cu is below Al — no reaction.
Answer: (c). Trap: picking (a) or (b) because the metals 'look reactive' — direction matters, not vibe.

segments.text: A N E E T speed trap on the activity series: which of four pairs will actually react?
The four options put a metal with a salt: copper with zinc sulphate, silver with copper sulphate, zinc with iron sulphate, and copper with aluminium sulphate.
The mental rule is one line: <curious> a metal reacts only if it sits above the salt's metal in the activity series. Check the direction before predicting anything.
Option a, copper with zinc sulphate: copper is below zinc, so no reaction.
Option b, silver with copper sulphate: silver is below copper, so no reaction.
Option c, zinc with iron sulphate: zinc is above iron, so it reacts — zinc plus iron sulphate gives zinc sulphate plus iron.
Option d, copper with aluminium sulphate: copper is below aluminium, so no reaction.
The answer is c. The trap is picking a or b because those metals feel reactive — but direction matters, not vibe. Only a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one, never the reverse.
Activity series पे एक N E E T speed trap: चार pairs में से कौन सा actually react करेगा?
चारों options एक metal को एक salt के साथ रखते हैं: copper zinc sulphate के साथ, silver copper sulphate के साथ, zinc iron sulphate के साथ, और copper aluminium sulphate के साथ।
Mental rule एक line है: <curious> एक metal तभी react करता है जब वो activity series में salt के metal से ऊपर बैठे। कुछ भी predict करने से पहले direction check करो।
Option a, copper zinc sulphate के साथ: copper zinc से नीचे है, तो no reaction।
Option b, silver copper sulphate के साथ: silver copper से नीचे है, तो no reaction।
Option c, zinc iron sulphate के साथ: zinc iron से ऊपर है, तो react करता है — zinc plus iron sulphate देता है zinc sulphate plus iron।
Option d, copper aluminium sulphate के साथ: copper aluminium से नीचे है, तो no reaction।
Answer c है। Trap है a या b चुनना क्योंकि वो metals reactive लगते हैं — पर direction matters, vibe नहीं। सिर्फ ज़्यादा reactive metal कम reactive को displace करता है, कभी उल्टा नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: Worked example (JEE Main): classify Cl2 + NaOH and its reverse

board_events.text: Classify and prove with oxidation numbers
Chlorine: $0$ in $Cl_2$; $-1$ in $NaCl$; $+5$ in $NaClO_3$.
The same element (Cl) starts at $0$ and ends both lower ($-1$) and higher ($+5$) → disproportionation.
Electron check: 5 Cl drop $0 \rightarrow -1$ (gain 5 e$^-$ total); 1 Cl climbs $0 \rightarrow +5$ (lose 5 e$^-$) — balanced.
Comproportionation is the reverse — two states converge back to $0$:
Answer: disproportionation; the reverse reaction is its comproportionation.

segments.text: A J E E Main classification that combines the family idea with an oxidation-number proof — chlorine reacting with hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide.
The reaction is three chlorine plus six sodium hydroxide giving five sodium chloride plus one sodium chlorate plus three water.
Assign chlorine's oxidation number across the equation: it is zero in chlorine gas, minus one in sodium chloride, and plus five in sodium chlorate.
There it is: <excited> the same element, chlorine, starts at zero and ends up both lower at minus one and higher at plus five. That is the fingerprint of disproportionation.

Confirm it with an electron check: five chlorine atoms drop from zero to minus one, gaining five electrons in total, while one chlorine climbs from zero to plus five, losing five — the electrons balance, so a single element really is splitting both ways.
The examiner then asks about the reverse. Comproportionation is exactly that reverse — two different states of chlorine converging back to zero.
Written out, five chloride plus one chlorate plus six hydrogen ions gives three chlorine plus three water, where minus one and plus five meet at zero.
So the answer: this is a disproportionation, and its reverse reaction is the matching comproportionation — two directions of the same chemistry.
एक J E E Main classification जो family idea को oxidation-number proof से combine करती है — chlorine hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide के साथ react करता है।
Reaction है three chlorine plus six sodium hydroxide देता है five sodium chloride plus one sodium chlorate plus three water।
Chlorine का oxidation number equation भर assign करो: यह chlorine gas में zero, sodium chloride में minus one, और sodium chlorate में plus five है।
वो रहा: <excited> वही element, chlorine, zero से शुरू होता है और दोनों lower minus one और higher plus five पे खत्म होता है। यह disproportionation का fingerprint है।

इसे electron check से confirm करो: पाँच chlorine atoms zero से minus one गिरते हैं, total पाँच electrons gain करते हुए, जबकि एक chlorine zero से plus five चढ़ता है, पाँच lose करते हुए — electrons balance होते हैं, तो एक single element सच में दोनों तरफ split हो रहा है।
Examiner फिर reverse के बारे में पूछता है। Comproportionation exactly वही reverse है — chlorine के दो अलग states zero पे वापस converge करते।
लिखा हुआ, five chloride plus one chlorate plus six hydrogen ions देता है three chlorine plus three water, जहाँ minus one और plus five zero पे मिलते हैं।
तो answer: यह एक disproportionation है, और इसका reverse reaction matching comproportionation है — एक ही chemistry की दो directions।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: Worked example (JEE Advanced): ammonium dichromate — intramolecular redox

board_events.text: Classify precisely: decomposition, disproportionation, or rarer?
Assign O.N.: in the reactant, N is $-3$ and Cr is $+6$; in the products, N in $N_2$ is $0$ and Cr in $Cr_2O_3$ is $+3$.
N: $-3 \rightarrow 0$ — oxidised (loses electrons).
Cr: $+6 \rightarrow +3$ — reduced (gains electrons).
Two DIFFERENT elements change oppositely inside one compound → intramolecular redox (a sub-class of decomposition).
Not disproportionation — that needs ONE element splitting; here N and Cr are distinct.
Answer: intramolecular (decomposition) redox — N oxidised, Cr reduced within the same compound.

segments.text: The J E E Advanced twist: classify ammonium dichromate's decomposition precisely — is it a simple decomposition, a disproportionation, or something rarer?
The reaction is ammonium dichromate heating to give nitrogen gas, chromium three oxide, and water.

Assign oxidation numbers carefully. In the reactant, nitrogen is minus three and chromium is plus six. In the products, nitrogen in nitrogen gas is zero, and chromium in chromium three oxide is plus three.
So nitrogen goes from minus three to zero — it is oxidised, losing electrons.
And chromium goes from plus six to plus three — it is reduced, gaining electrons.

Here is the precise point: <curious> two different elements change in opposite directions inside the same compound. That is a special case called intramolecular redox, a sub-class of decomposition redox.
It is not disproportionation, because disproportionation requires one single element splitting into a higher and a lower state — here nitrogen and chromium are two distinct elements.
So the precise answer: this is an intramolecular decomposition redox, with nitrogen oxidised and chromium reduced within the same compound.
J E E Advanced twist: ammonium dichromate के decomposition को precisely classify करो — यह simple decomposition है, disproportionation, या कुछ rarer?
Reaction है ammonium dichromate गरम होकर nitrogen gas, chromium three oxide, और water देता है।
Oxidation numbers carefully assign करो। Reactant में, nitrogen minus three और chromium plus six है। Products में, nitrogen gas में nitrogen zero, और chromium three oxide में chromium plus three है।
तो nitrogen minus three से zero जाता है — यह oxidised होता है, electrons खोते हुए।
और chromium plus six से plus three जाता है — यह reduced होता है, electrons gain करते हुए।

यह रहा precise point: <curious> दो अलग elements एक ही compound के अंदर opposite directions में बदलते हैं। यह एक special case है जिसे intramolecular redox कहते हैं, decomposition redox का एक sub-class।
यह disproportionation नहीं है, क्योंकि disproportionation को एक single element का higher और lower state में splitting चाहिए — यहाँ nitrogen और chromium दो distinct elements हैं।
तो precise answer: यह एक intramolecular decomposition redox है, nitrogen oxidised और chromium reduced एक ही compound के अंदर।

sections.subtopic: Types of Redox Reactions & Redox in Action
sections.title: Pitfalls & pro-tips: classify fast, confirm with O.N.

board_events.text: The classification traps
Assuming all combinations/decompositions are redox — $CaO + CO_2$ and $CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2$ involve no O.N. change.
Getting displacement direction backwards — only a more reactive species displaces a less reactive one; copper never displaces zinc.
Calling a two-element reaction a disproportionation — when two different elements move oppositely in one compound, it is intramolecular redox.
Stock-notation slips — use Roman numerals in parentheses with no $+$ sign: iron(III), not iron(+3) or iron(3).
Pro-tip: count first, confirm with O.N.
Glance at the count of reactants/products (2→1 combination, 1→many decomposition, element-swaps displacement), then confirm with one O.N. check.
Disproportionation fingerprint: one element appearing in THREE different O.N. states across the equation — its start, plus a higher and a lower.

segments.text: Let's close the chapter's classification work with the four traps and the one habit that classifies fast.

First, and the big one: assuming every combination or decomposition is redox. Calcium oxide plus carbon dioxide, and calcium carbonate decomposing back, involve no oxidation-number change at all. Always assign oxidation numbers first.
Second: getting the displacement direction backwards. Only a more reactive species displaces a less reactive one — copper never displaces zinc. Check the series before you predict.
Third: calling a two-element reaction a disproportionation. When two different elements move in opposite directions inside one compound, that is intramolecular redox, not disproportionation.
Fourth: Stock-notation slips. Use Roman numerals in parentheses with no plus sign — iron three, never iron plus three or iron three in ordinary digits.
Now the pro-tip that ties it together. To classify fast, glance first at the count of reactants and products.
Two into one suggests combination, one into many suggests decomposition, and an element swapping in suggests displacement — then confirm with a single oxidation-number check.

And for disproportionation, look for the unmistakable fingerprint: <whisper> one element appearing in three different oxidation states across the equation — its starting state, plus one higher and one lower.
Chapter के classification work को चार traps और एक habit के साथ बंद करते हैं जो fast classify करती है।

पहला, और बड़ा: हर combination या decomposition को redox मानना। Calcium oxide plus carbon dioxide, और calcium carbonate का वापस decompose होना, में कोई oxidation-number change है ही नहीं। हमेशा पहले oxidation numbers assign करो।
दूसरा: displacement direction उल्टा करना। सिर्फ ज़्यादा reactive species कम reactive को displace करती है — copper कभी zinc को displace नहीं करता। Predict करने से पहले series check करो।
तीसरा: दो-element reaction को disproportionation कहना। जब दो अलग elements एक compound में opposite directions में move करें, वो intramolecular redox है, disproportionation नहीं।
चौथा: Stock-notation slips। Parentheses में Roman numerals use करो बिना plus sign — iron three, कभी iron plus three या ordinary digits में iron three नहीं।
अब वो pro-tip जो सब जोड़ता है। Fast classify करने को, पहले reactants और products की count पे नज़र डालो।
दो का एक combination suggest करता है, एक का कई decomposition, और एक element का swap in होना displacement — फिर एक single oxidation-number check से confirm करो।
और disproportionation के लिए, वो unmistakable fingerprint ढूँढो: <whisper> एक element equation भर तीन अलग oxidation states में — उसका starting state, plus एक higher और एक lower।

sections.title: Formula recap: every engine of the chapter in one place

board_events.text: The whole chapter's working relations

board_events.latex: M_1 n_1 V_1 = M_2 n_2 V_2, \qquad N = M \times n \qquad (\text{7.3: titration})

board_events.text: Every one of these is the same electron-conservation idea wearing a different hat.

segments.text: Let's gather every working relation from the chapter into one place, so you can revise the machinery at a glance.
From subtopic one: the charge-balance rule. The sum of oxidation numbers over all atoms equals the net charge on the species — this alone lets you assign any unknown oxidation number.
From subtopic two: the balancing principle. Electrons lost equal electrons gained — the single law behind both the oxidation-number method and the ion-electron method.
From subtopic three, titrations: molarity times n times volume on one side equals the same on the other, and normality equals molarity times the n-factor.
Then the cell E M F: cathode potential minus anode potential, both as reduction potentials.
The energy link: the standard Gibbs free energy change is minus n times Faraday's constant times the cell E M F, with Faraday's constant ninety-six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole.

And the equilibrium and Nernst pair: log K is n times the cell E M F over zero point zero five nine one, while the actual E M F is the standard value minus zero point zero five nine one over n times log Q.
Keep the n-factors handy too: permanganate is five in acid and three in neutral, dichromate six, oxalate two, and iron one.
Step back and notice the unity: <curious> every one of these relations is the same electron-conservation idea, just wearing a different hat.
Chapter की हर working relation को एक जगह इकट्ठा करते हैं, ताकि तुम machinery एक नज़र में revise कर सको।
Subtopic one से: charge-balance rule। सारे atoms के oxidation numbers का sum species के net charge के बराबर — यह अकेले किसी भी unknown oxidation number को assign करने देता है।
Subtopic two से: balancing principle। Electrons lost equal electrons gained — वो single law जो oxidation-number method और ion-electron method दोनों के पीछे है।
Subtopic three से, titrations: एक side molarity times n times volume equal दूसरी side वही, और normality equals molarity times n-factor।
फिर cell E M F: cathode potential minus anode potential, दोनों reduction potentials की तरह।
Energy link: standard Gibbs free energy change minus n times Faraday's constant times cell E M F है, Faraday's constant ninety-six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole के साथ।
और equilibrium तथा Nernst pair: log K n times cell E M F over zero point zero five nine one है, जबकि actual E M F standard value minus zero point zero five nine one over n times log Q।
n-factors भी handy रखो: permanganate acid में पाँच और neutral में तीन, dichromate छह, oxalate दो, और iron एक।
पीछे हटकर unity notice करो: <curious> इनमें से हर एक relation वही electron-conservation idea है, बस अलग hat पहने हुए।

sections.subtopic: Redox Reactions — Consolidation
sections.title: Cheat sheet: fast recall for the whole chapter

board_events.text: Redox Reactions — rapid recall
Three lenses: oxidation = add O / lose H / lose e$^-$ / $\uparrow$ O.N.; reduction is the reverse. $\sum$(O.N.) = net charge.
Assign O.N.: Group 1 $+1$, Group 2 $+2$, Al $+3$, F $-1$; O $-2$ (peroxide $-1$, $OF_2$ $+2$); H $+1$ (hydride $-1$). Fractional O.N. = average only.
Agents: oxidant is REDUCED (gains e$^-$); reductant is OXIDISED (loses e$^-$). The agent does the opposite to itself.
Balancing: O.N. method or ion-electron method; medium tools — acid $H^+/H_2O$, base $OH^-/H_2O$. Basic shortcut: balance as acid, then add $OH^-$.
$MnO_4^-$ electron memory: acid $5$, neutral $3$, strong base $1$ \u2014 '5\u20133\u20131 as the base grows on'.
Cells: An Ox / Red Cat; $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cat} - E^\circ_{an}$; positive $\Rightarrow$ spontaneous; $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$.

Four types + reactivity series ($K \ldots Au$). Disproportionation (one element splits) vs comproportionation (reverse) vs intramolecular (two elements). Mnemonics: OIL RIG; 'count first, confirm with O.N.'

segments.text: Finally, the one-screen cheat sheet — everything condensed for the night before the exam.

The three lenses, all equivalent: oxidation is adding oxygen, losing hydrogen, losing electrons, or raising the oxidation number — reduction is the reverse. And the master rule, sum of oxidation numbers equals the net charge.

For assigning: group one is plus one, group two plus two, aluminium plus three, fluorine minus one; oxygen minus two except peroxide minus one and oxygen difluoride plus two; hydrogen plus one except minus one in hydrides. A fractional value is only an average.
On agents, say it once more so it sticks: <whisper> the oxidant is reduced and gains electrons, the reductant is oxidised and loses electrons. The agent does the opposite to itself.

For balancing, use either the oxidation-number method or the ion-electron method, with water and hydrogen ions in acid, water and hydroxide in base — and the shortcut of balancing as acid, then adding hydroxide.
Keep the permanganate electron memory: five in acid, three in neutral, one in strong base — five, three, one as the base grows on.
For cells: An Ox, Red Cat; cell E M F is cathode minus anode; positive means spontaneous; and the free energy is minus n F times the E M F.

And the four types with the reactivity series from potassium to gold: distinguish disproportionation, where one element splits, from comproportionation, its reverse, and from intramolecular redox, where two different elements change. Carry the mnemonics — O I L R I G, and count first, then confirm with an oxidation-number check. That is the whole chapter in one breath.
आखिर में, one-screen cheat sheet — exam से एक रात पहले के लिए सब कुछ condensed।

तीन lenses, सब equivalent: oxidation है oxygen add करना, hydrogen lose करना, electrons lose करना, या oxidation number बढ़ाना — reduction उल्टा। और master rule, sum of oxidation numbers equals net charge।

Assign करने के लिए: group one plus one, group two plus two, aluminium plus three, fluorine minus one; oxygen minus two सिवाय peroxide minus one और oxygen difluoride plus two; hydrogen plus one सिवाय hydrides में minus one। Fractional value सिर्फ average है।
Agents पे, एक बार फिर बोलो ताकि यह stick हो: <whisper> oxidant reduce होता है और electrons gain करता है, reductant oxidise होता है और electrons lose करता है। Agent अपने साथ उल्टा करता है।
Balancing के लिए, oxidation-number method या ion-electron method use करो, acid में water और hydrogen ions, base में water और hydroxide — और shortcut acid की तरह balance करके फिर hydroxide add करना।
Permanganate electron memory रखो: acid में पाँच, neutral में तीन, strong base में एक — five, three, one as the base grows on।
Cells के लिए: An Ox, Red Cat; cell E M F cathode minus anode है; positive मतलब spontaneous; और free energy minus n F times E M F है।

और चार types reactivity series potassium से gold के साथ: disproportionation, जहाँ एक element splits, को comproportionation, इसके reverse, और intramolecular redox, जहाँ दो अलग elements बदलते हैं, से distinguish करो। Mnemonics carry करो — O I L R I G, और count first, फिर oxidation-number check से confirm। यह पूरा chapter एक साँस में।
